item.title: 1Password SSH Agent and CLI: Read-Only AI Agent Access
item.description: Design a read-only SSH workflow with 1Password CLI, the SSH Agent, and MCP. Use synthetic commands, narrow permissions, and human approval before live testing.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>A command-line agent needs useful access, not a copy of every credential.</strong> This guide presents a bounded design for 1Password CLI, the 1Password SSH Agent, Bitbucket Git access, and Model Context Protocol (MCP). The first workflow uses synthetic names, read-only actions, and human approval at the SSH boundary.</p> <p>The key distinction is simple. <strong>Interactive SSH uses consent through the 1Password SSH Agent. Unattended automation needs a separate identity, narrow access, and a different key lifecycle.</strong> Do not treat an MCP connection as permission to run either workflow.</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Private-key protection:</strong> The 1Password SSH Agent performs SSH authentication while keeping private keys inside the 1Password app.</li> <li><strong>Public-key handling:</strong> Publish only a public key to Bitbucket or a remote account. Keep the private half in an SSH Key item.</li> <li><strong>Interactive consent:</strong> A person approves a client or terminal session before the SSH Agent uses a key.</li> <li><strong>Unattended separation:</strong> A scheduled job needs a dedicated service account and a narrow vault scope. An interactive SSH Agent approval does not satisfy this need.</li> <li><strong>MCP boundaries:</strong> MCP connects an agent to tools and resources. The client, server, operating system, and 1Password policy still control access.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Prerequisites:</strong> Install 1Password 8 and 1Password CLI 2.20.0 or later. Sign in through a supported 1Password account. Use an OpenSSH client. Create a test Bitbucket repository or another non-production target. Keep a second administrative path available for rollback.</p> <p><strong>Time:</strong> 30 to 45 minutes for a design review and synthetic walkthrough.</p> <p><strong>Difficulty:</strong> Intermediate. You need basic Git, SSH, shell, and access-control knowledge.</p> <p>This guide covers design and planning. The linked Bitbucket article covers Bitbucket-specific access boundaries. This guide does not test a live account, create a real key, connect to a real host, or register a real MCP server. Every identifier below is synthetic. <strong>Replace placeholders only inside your own controlled environment.</strong></p> <p><strong>Version posture:</strong> Use 1Password 8 and <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password CLI 2.20.0 or later"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/manage-keys"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/manage-keys" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password CLI 2.20.0 or later</a> </span> for this workflow. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password CLI 1 is deprecated"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/cli/upgrade/"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/cli/upgrade/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password CLI 1 is deprecated</a> </span> . <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password 7 retires in early 2027"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.1password.com/add-account/"> <a href="https://support.1password.com/add-account/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password 7 retires in early 2027</a> </span> . SSH-key generation, import, and sharing require 1Password 8. Confirm the installed Git, OpenSSH, MCP host, and MCP server versions before testing. The examples below remain untested.</p> <p>A <strong>vault</strong> is a protected 1Password collection of items. <strong>OpenSSH</strong> is the SSH client and server software used by many operating systems. <strong>MCP</strong>, or Model Context Protocol, connects an agent to approved tools or resources.</p> <h2 id="why-keep-private-keys-unread"> <a href="#why-keep-private-keys-unread" title="Why Keep Private Keys Unread">Why Keep Private Keys Unread</a> <a href="#why-keep-private-keys-unread" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Keep Private Keys Unread">#</a> </h2> <p>An SSH key pair has a public key and a private key. A remote Git service or server stores the public key. The client proves possession of the private key during authentication. The private key does not need to travel to the remote service.</p> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password SSH Agent"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/agent"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/agent" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password SSH Agent</a> </span> extends this model. Its documentation says SSH and Git clients authenticate through the agent while the private key stays in the 1Password app. The client receives a signing result, not a private-key file.</p> <p>This boundary reduces several exposure paths:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Source control:</strong> A private key does not enter a repository or a pull request.</li> <li><strong>Shell history:</strong> A private-key value does not appear in a command argument.</li> <li><strong>Temporary files:</strong> A script does not need to write a private key to <code>~/.ssh/</code>.</li> <li><strong>Agent context:</strong> A large language model (LLM) does not need the private-key text to request an SSH operation.</li> <li><strong>Accidental reuse:</strong> A copied key does not remain in an old workspace after a task ends.</li> </ul> <p>The boundary does not make SSH harmless. A process with permission to use the agent socket might perform actions as the approved key. Host-key verification, remote account limits, repository permissions, command policy, and process isolation still matter.</p> <p><em>The private-key boundary protects key material. The boundary does not approve a remote command or prove the target host is trusted.</em></p> <h2 id="interactive-ssh-consent"> <a href="#interactive-ssh-consent" title="Interactive SSH Consent">Interactive SSH Consent</a> <a href="#interactive-ssh-consent" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Interactive SSH Consent">#</a> </h2> <p>Configure a dedicated vault for agent keys. Use the SSH Agent configuration file to select the smallest key set and a host-specific key. Do not expose every eligible key from every built-in vault to an automation process.</p> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password SSH Agent security model"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/agent/security"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/agent/security" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password SSH Agent security model</a> </span> ties approval to a key and a requesting process. The prompt identifies the process and key. The person then approves the request through the configured authentication method.</p> <p>1Password documents several approval scopes. Per-key and per-application approval is the default. A terminal-session scope narrows approval to a tab or session. Per-request approval asks again for every request. An all-process approval option exists, but this option gives every process under the current operating-system user access for the session.</p> <p><strong>Use the narrowest approval scope suitable for the task.</strong> A systems-administration agent should run in a dedicated terminal or sandbox. Do not approve every process when a single terminal session is enough.</p> <p>The approval session is not a permanent grant. 1Password records the authorization for the configured period or until the app locks or quits. When the app is locked, the agent does not retain private keys for later use. The SSH Agent process continues in the background when the supported setting is enabled while 1Password is closed, but a new signing request requires 1Password to be unlocked.</p> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password SSH setup guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/get-started"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/get-started" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password SSH setup guide</a> </span> shows the general flow: generate or import a key, publish the public key, enable the SSH Agent, configure the SSH client, run an SSH or Git command, and approve the request. The exact socket path differs by operating system. Use the current platform instructions instead of copying a path from another machine.</p> <p>The 1Password app must be unlocked before a new signing request succeeds. The agent process might continue in the background while the app is closed. A locked app does not release private-key material for signing.</p> <h2 id="public-keys-and-bitbucket"> <a href="#public-keys-and-bitbucket" title="Public Keys and Bitbucket">Public Keys and Bitbucket</a> <a href="#public-keys-and-bitbucket" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Public Keys and Bitbucket">#</a> </h2> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password key-management guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/manage-keys"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/manage-keys" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password key-management guide</a> </span> documents SSH Key items, key generation, key import, public keys, fingerprints, and private keys. The CLI example uses <code>op item create --category ssh</code> to create an SSH Key item. 1Password CLI generates an Ed25519 key by default for this example and redacts the private key in its output.</p> <p>Bitbucket Cloud uses the normal Git and OpenSSH command-line workflow. Its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="command-line guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/find-the-command-line/"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/find-the-command-line/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >command-line guide</a> </span> describes Git operations from a local repository. Its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="SSH configuration guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/configure-ssh-and-two-step-verification"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/configure-ssh-and-two-step-verification" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >SSH configuration guide</a> </span> lists SSH remote forms and supported public-key formats.</p> <p><strong>Treat Bitbucket as the public-key consumer.</strong> Register the public key or fingerprint through the approved Bitbucket account or repository setting. Keep the private key in 1Password. The Git client asks the SSH Agent to sign. The client does not read a private-key file.</p> <p>For the Bitbucket access-key scope, registration path, and read-only Git test, see <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Bitbucket Cloud SSH Keys and Git CLI: Read-Only Access for AI Agents"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/bitbucket-cloud-ssh-keys-git-cli-mcp-agent-automation/"> <a href="/articles/bitbucket-cloud-ssh-keys-git-cli-mcp-agent-automation/" rel="follow me" >Bitbucket Cloud SSH Keys and Git CLI: Read-Only Access for AI Agents</a> </span> .</p> <p>The Bitbucket documentation calls this a Git CLI workflow. This article does not assume a separate Bitbucket MCP server or a product named Bitbucket CLI. A Bitbucket-specific CLI needs its own current documentation and its own permission review.</p> <h2 id="the-agent-and-mcp-boundary"> <a href="#the-agent-and-mcp-boundary" title="The Agent and MCP Boundary">The Agent and MCP Boundary</a> <a href="#the-agent-and-mcp-boundary" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The Agent and MCP Boundary">#</a> </h2> <p>Use the current <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MCP specification"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28"> <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MCP specification</a> </span> when reviewing a new server.</p> <p>The 2025-06-18 specification URL in the following background paragraph is a historical version. Use the 2026-07-28 specification for new reviews.</p> <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MCP"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18"> <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MCP</a> </span> standardizes connections between an LLM application, a client connector, and a server. A server offers tools, resources, or prompts. The specification also says hosts must obtain user consent before exposing data or invoking tools.</p> <p><strong>MCP itself does not grant permissions.</strong> An MCP tool still runs within the permissions of its server process, operating-system user, network path, cloud account, and configured credentials. A tool description is not an authorization policy.</p> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password Security for AI documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/security-for-ai"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/security-for-ai" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password Security for AI documentation</a> </span> describes an Environments MCP Server and secure MCP configuration patterns. The same page describes runtime loading of MCP configuration values from 1Password. These pages do not define a generic 1Password SSH-key MCP product or a universal SSH workflow for every agent client.</p> <p>Use MCP as a narrow control surface:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Read tools:</strong> Inspect service status, repository metadata, or approved logs.</li> <li><strong>Plan tools:</strong> Prepare a command or change record without executing the command.</li> <li><strong>Approval tools:</strong> Request a human decision before a remote write.</li> <li><strong>Write tools:</strong> Keep disabled until the target, command, scope, and rollback plan are explicit.</li> </ul> <p>The agent should receive references, metadata, and operation results. <strong>The agent should not receive private-key text, a vault-wide item dump, or an unrestricted shell.</strong></p> <h2 id="a-safe-first-policy"> <a href="#a-safe-first-policy" title="A Safe First Policy">A Safe First Policy</a> <a href="#a-safe-first-policy" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A Safe First Policy">#</a> </h2> <p>Start with a written policy before enabling an agent. Keep the policy close to the MCP configuration, but do not place credentials in the file.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-yaml" data-lang="yaml"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#f92672">agent_policy</span>: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">purpose</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"Read-only repository and system inspection"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">identities</span>: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">interactive_ssh</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"1Password SSH Agent with per-terminal consent"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">unattended_jobs</span>: <span style="color:#e6db74">"Dedicated service account with one narrow vault"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">allowed</span>: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Read repository metadata through Git"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Read approved service status and logs"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Run one synthetic SSH connectivity check"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">approval_required</span>: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Any remote write"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Any package, firewall, clock, or service change"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Any new host-key acceptance"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Any private-key export"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">denied</span>: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Read or print private-key fields"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"List every vault or every item"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Write tokens or secrets to shell profiles"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Run arbitrary commands from tool output"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#f92672">rollback</span>: </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Revoke the service account"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Remove the public key from the target"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Disable the MCP server entry"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> - <span style="color:#e6db74">"Lock 1Password and end the agent session"</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>This policy is an example, not a 1Password configuration format. Store the real policy in the control plane used by your agent client. Review every tool against the policy before enabling each tool.</p> <h2 id="service-accounts-and-secret-references"> <a href="#service-accounts-and-secret-references" title="Service Accounts and Secret References">Service Accounts and Secret References</a> <a href="#service-accounts-and-secret-references" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Service Accounts and Secret References">#</a> </h2> <p>A <strong>service account</strong> gives an automated process its own identity. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password CLI script guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/cli/secrets-scripts"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/cli/secrets-scripts" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password CLI script guide</a> </span> recommends service accounts for least-privilege access to selected vaults. This separates an unattended job from a person’s SSO, MFA, vault inventory, and daily account.</p> <p>A <strong>secret reference</strong> names a value without placing the value in source. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password CLI reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/cli/reference"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/cli/reference" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password CLI reference</a> </span> uses the form <code>op://vault/item/field</code>. The reference is safe to store only when the surrounding process still has narrow access. A reference does not bypass policy.</p> <p>Use <code>op read</code> when one command needs one value. Use <code>op run</code> when a child process needs a controlled set of runtime values. Use <code>op item create</code> when a new SSH Key item needs to exist in the approved vault.</p> <p>Do not confuse runtime injection with private-key protection. An API token passed as an environment variable is still visible to the child process. A private key passed through an environment variable is worse because the value expands exposure to process inspection, crash reports, debug output, shell tracing, and accidental logging.</p> <p><strong>Prefer a reference in source and a runtime value in the smallest possible process.</strong> Keep the process short-lived. Disable shell tracing. Do not print the environment. Remove temporary files after a failed run.</p> <h2 id="safe-first-workflow"> <a href="#safe-first-workflow" title="Safe First Workflow">Safe First Workflow</a> <a href="#safe-first-workflow" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Safe First Workflow">#</a> </h2> <p>The sequence below separates public-key registration, interactive SSH, MCP discovery, and unattended design.</p> <h3 id="1-define-the-target"> <a href="#1-define-the-target" title="1. Define the target">1. Define the target</a> <a href="#1-define-the-target" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="1. Define the target">#</a> </h3> <p>Write down the target class, remote account, intended repository or command, host-key source, approval owner, and rollback action. Use a synthetic record during the first exercise.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>target_class: test-repository </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>remote_account: git </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>operation: read-only connectivity check </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>host_key_source: approved administrator record </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>approval_owner: named operator </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>rollback: remove public key and revoke test identity </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Expected result, untested:</strong> The record identifies one target and one operation. The record does not contain a hostname, IP address, token, private key, or personal data.</p> <h3 id="2-create-or-select-the-ssh-key-item"> <a href="#2-create-or-select-the-ssh-key-item" title="2. Create or select the SSH Key item">2. Create or select the SSH Key item</a> <a href="#2-create-or-select-the-ssh-key-item" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="2. Create or select the SSH Key item">#</a> </h3> <p>The official <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password SSH key guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/manage-keys"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/manage-keys" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password SSH key guide</a> </span> documents the CLI creation pattern. The command below uses a synthetic title and named test vault.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>op item create --category ssh --ssh-generate-key<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>ed25519 --vault <span style="color:#e6db74">"synthetic-test-vault"</span> --title <span style="color:#e6db74">"synthetic-agent-admin-key"</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Expected output, untested:</strong> 1Password creates an SSH Key item in the named test vault and redacts the private key in the terminal output. The command changes 1Password state. The exact human-readable output depends on the CLI version and sign-in state.</p> <p>Capture the returned item identifier in the test record without copying the private-key field. Use the identifier or the exact item title for later field-specific reads only after the item schema is confirmed.</p> <p>Do not redirect this output to a shared log. Capture only the item identifier, public-key fingerprint, and approval record when the local procedure supports safe structured output.</p> <h3 id="3-handle-the-public-key"> <a href="#3-handle-the-public-key" title="3. Handle the public key">3. Handle the public key</a> <a href="#3-handle-the-public-key" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="3. Handle the public key">#</a> </h3> <p>Open the SSH Key item in 1Password and use its Copy Public Key action. Use a field-specific reference only after you confirm the public-key field label in your own account. Do not dump the complete item.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>PUBLIC_KEY_REF<span style="color:#f92672">=</span><span style="color:#e6db74">"op://synthetic-test-vault/synthetic-agent-admin-key/synthetic-public-key-field"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>op read <span style="color:#e6db74">"</span>$PUBLIC_KEY_REF<span style="color:#e6db74">"</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Expected output, untested:</strong> One synthetic OpenSSH public-key line or a public-key value from the confirmed field. The placeholder field name above is not a promise about your item’s field label.</p> <p>Register the public key in the approved Bitbucket account, Bitbucket repository, or remote account. Never paste the matching private key into Bitbucket. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Bitbucket SSH guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/configure-ssh-and-two-step-verification"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/configure-ssh-and-two-step-verification" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Bitbucket SSH guide</a> </span> also recommends recording the Bitbucket host key before the first connection.</p> <p>For Bitbucket, fetch the published host-key record and compare the record with an independent trusted copy before adding a line to <code>~/.ssh/known_hosts</code>. Use strict host checking after the comparison passes. Do not accept a changed host key during an agent run.</p> <h3 id="4-enable-interactive-ssh"> <a href="#4-enable-interactive-ssh" title="4. Enable interactive SSH">4. Enable interactive SSH</a> <a href="#4-enable-interactive-ssh" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="4. Enable interactive SSH">#</a> </h3> <p>Turn on the 1Password SSH Agent in the desktop app. Configure OpenSSH with the platform-specific <code>IdentityAgent</code> or <code>SSH_AUTH_SOCK</code> value from the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="official setup guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/get-started"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/get-started" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >official setup guide</a> </span> . Limit the first test to one repository or one non-production account.</p> <p>On macOS or Linux, set the socket from the platform setup guide and run <code>ssh-add -l</code>. On Windows, use the supported named-pipe configuration and verify available keys through the 1Password SSH Agent interface or a documented Windows SSH test. Do not present <code>ssh-add -l</code> as a cross-platform verification command.</p> <p>On macOS or Linux only:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>ssh-add -l </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>git ls-remote <span style="color:#e6db74">"<repository-ssh-url>"</span> HEAD </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Expected output, untested:</strong> On macOS or Linux, <code>ssh-add -l</code> lists fingerprints from the active agent. On Windows, use the documented named-pipe test or the 1Password SSH Agent interface. A successful Git read returns a commit reference. The repository placeholder above requires replacement in a controlled test.</p> <p>The command uses a repository placeholder. Replace the placeholder only in a controlled test. <strong>Do not approve a prompt for a target or process you did not expect.</strong></p> <h3 id="5-add-mcp-after-the-ssh-path-works"> <a href="#5-add-mcp-after-the-ssh-path-works" title="5. Add MCP after the SSH path works">5. Add MCP after the SSH path works</a> <a href="#5-add-mcp-after-the-ssh-path-works" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="5. Add MCP after the SSH path works">#</a> </h3> <p>First verify the SSH client and target without MCP. Then add one read-only MCP server or local connector. Give the agent a tool such as <code>read_status</code> or <code>prepare_command</code>. Do not start with a general shell tool.</p> <p>The MCP configuration should reference runtime values through the client’s supported environment mechanism. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password AI security guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/security-for-ai"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/security-for-ai" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password AI security guide</a> </span> describes replacing plaintext MCP configuration tokens with environment variables loaded from 1Password. <strong>Keep the reference or variable name in configuration. Keep the resolved value out of the agent transcript.</strong></p> <p>This section describes a design, not a tested MCP configuration. No client, server, transport, version, or fixture is pinned here. Validate one read-only server in a separate test profile before connecting an agent to a production system.</p> <h3 id="6-record-the-result"> <a href="#6-record-the-result" title="6. Record the result">6. Record the result</a> <a href="#6-record-the-result" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="6. Record the result">#</a> </h3> <p>Record the target class, tool name, approval decision, public-key fingerprint, command outcome, and cleanup result. Omit secret values. Mark each output as observed or expected.</p> <p><strong>Expected result, untested:</strong> The agent reads status, proposes a bounded command, receives explicit approval for the SSH request, completes the read-only operation, and produces a record without private-key text.</p> <h2 id="synthetic-command-sequence"> <a href="#synthetic-command-sequence" title="Synthetic Command Sequence">Synthetic Command Sequence</a> <a href="#synthetic-command-sequence" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Synthetic Command Sequence">#</a> </h2> <p>The following sequence shows the order without using real infrastructure. These commands are examples only. They were not run during article preparation.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>op --version </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>op item create --category ssh --ssh-generate-key<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>ed25519 --vault <span style="color:#e6db74">"synthetic-test-vault"</span> --title <span style="color:#e6db74">"synthetic-agent-admin-key"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>op read <span style="color:#e6db74">"op://synthetic-test-vault/synthetic-agent-admin-key/synthetic-public-key-field"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># macOS or Linux only</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ssh-add -l </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>git ls-remote <span style="color:#e6db74">"<repository-ssh-url>"</span> HEAD </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Expected output, untested:</strong></p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-text" data-lang="text"><span style="display:flex;"><span>2.x.y </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>SSH Key item created. Private key: redacted </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ssh-ed25519 AAAA<synthetic-public-key> synthetic-key-label </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>256 SHA256:<synthetic-fingerprint> synthetic-agent-admin-key (ED25519) </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><synthetic-commit-id> HEAD </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The output block is illustrative. The block does not represent a run against a 1Password account, Bitbucket, Git provider, or remote host. A production record should store only approved metadata and a success or failure state.</p> <h2 id="interactive-versus-unattended-access"> <a href="#interactive-versus-unattended-access" title="Interactive Versus Unattended Access">Interactive Versus Unattended Access</a> <a href="#interactive-versus-unattended-access" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Interactive Versus Unattended Access">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Access mode</th> <th>Identity</th> <th>Private-key path</th> <th>Approval model</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Interactive SSH</strong></td> <td>Human account through 1Password SSH Agent</td> <td>Private key stays in the 1Password app</td> <td>Human approves a process, terminal session, or request</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Scheduled read</strong></td> <td>Dedicated service account</td> <td><code>op run</code> supplies narrow runtime values</td> <td>Job policy and service-account scope</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Scheduled SSH</strong></td> <td>Dedicated automation identity</td> <td>Key export remains a last-resort design</td> <td>Job isolation, short lifetime, host restriction, and rotation</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Agent write</strong></td> <td>Human or task-specific identity</td> <td>Depends on the approved integration</td> <td>Human approval before each defined change</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><em>Do not schedule a workflow around an interactive SSH Agent prompt. Use a separate automation design or keep the step human-operated.</em></p> <p>For unattended jobs, create a service account with access to one vault or a small set of items. Give the job one purpose. Use a dedicated repository or server account. Add host-key verification. Set an execution timeout. Log action metadata without secrets. Rotate or revoke the identity after the test.</p> <p>If an unattended job truly needs an SSH private key, use a dedicated automation key with a narrow remote account and a documented end date. Fetching the private key with <code>op read</code> still exports key material across a process boundary. This design has a larger blast radius than the 1Password SSH Agent. Prefer a platform identity, deploy service, or other workload identity when the target supports one.</p> <h2 id="why-plaintext-environment-variables-raise-risk"> <a href="#why-plaintext-environment-variables-raise-risk" title="Why Plaintext Environment Variables Raise Risk">Why Plaintext Environment Variables Raise Risk</a> <a href="#why-plaintext-environment-variables-raise-risk" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Why Plaintext Environment Variables Raise Risk">#</a> </h2> <p>Environment variables keep secrets out of source files, but they do not make secrets invisible. A child process reads its environment. Process inspection, crash handlers, debug output, shell tracing, and copied command records might expose values.</p> <p>1Password documents <code>op run</code> as a runtime method for loading references into a subprocess. Use <code>op run</code> for values a process truly needs. Keep the child process short-lived and restrict its command. Do not pass a private key through <code>SSH_PRIVATE_KEY</code>, <code>KEY</code>, or a similar variable when the SSH Agent removes the need for export.</p> <p>The safer order is:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Use the SSH Agent</strong> for interactive SSH.</li> <li><strong>Use public-key registration</strong> for Bitbucket or the remote account.</li> <li><strong>Use <code>op run</code></strong> for a narrow unattended child process.</li> <li><strong>Use <code>op read</code></strong> for one value when a child process does not need a full environment.</li> <li><strong>Export a private key</strong> only after a written exception, narrow scope, cleanup plan, and rotation plan.</li> </ol> <h2 id="decision-table"> <a href="#decision-table" title="Decision Table">Decision Table</a> <a href="#decision-table" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Decision Table">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Need</th> <th>Preferred path</th> <th>Reason to stop or redesign</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>Human runs Git over SSH</td> <td>1Password SSH Agent</td> <td>Stop if the prompt names an unexpected process or key</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Register a repository key</td> <td>Read or autofill the public key</td> <td>Never copy the private key into the repository service</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Agent reads service status</td> <td>Read-only MCP tool with OS-level scope</td> <td>Stop if the tool exposes an unrestricted shell</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Agent proposes a remote change</td> <td>Plan tool followed by human approval</td> <td>Stop if target, command, or rollback is unclear</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Job reads one API token</td> <td>Service account plus <code>op read</code> or <code>op run</code></td> <td>Stop if the token enters source, logs, or a global profile</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Job needs SSH access</td> <td>Workload identity or dedicated automation key</td> <td>Stop if the job requires a personal key or broad account</td> </tr> <tr> <td>MCP config needs a token</td> <td>Runtime reference loaded by the supported client</td> <td>Stop if a plaintext token is committed to config</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="failure-handling"> <a href="#failure-handling" title="Failure Handling">Failure Handling</a> <a href="#failure-handling" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Failure Handling">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Unexpected SSH consent prompt:</strong> Deny the prompt. Check the process name, terminal session, key fingerprint, repository target, and host key. Review the SSH client configuration before retrying.</p> <p><strong>No SSH Agent socket:</strong> Confirm the 1Password desktop app is installed through a supported method, the SSH Agent is enabled, and the client uses the platform-specific socket. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="official SSH Agent page"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/agent"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/agent" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >official SSH Agent page</a> </span> lists operating-system requirements and socket setup links.</p> <p><strong>Public-key authentication fails:</strong> Check the selected public key, remote account, repository permission, host key, and SSH configuration. Use a public fingerprint comparison. Do not solve the error by exporting an unrelated private key.</p> <p><strong><code>op read</code> denies access:</strong> Check the service-account vault scope, item identifier, field reference, sign-in state, and item status. Reduce the reference to one approved item. Do not widen the vault grant as a first response.</p> <p><strong><code>op run</code> exposes a value:</strong> Stop the job. Preserve only the minimum incident record. Remove copied logs and temporary files according to your retention procedure. Rotate the affected secret or key. Review shell tracing, process inspection, crash reports, and MCP transcript retention.</p> <p><strong>MCP tool behaves unexpectedly:</strong> Treat tool output as untrusted data. Stop before executing commands suggested by the output. Inspect the server source, configuration, permissions, and transport. The MCP host must obtain user consent. The specification also provides implementor guidance for consent and access controls, but the protocol does not replace your review.</p> <h2 id="rollback-and-removal"> <a href="#rollback-and-removal" title="Rollback and Removal">Rollback and Removal</a> <a href="#rollback-and-removal" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Rollback and Removal">#</a> </h2> <p>Rollback starts with access removal, not file deletion.</p> <ol> <li><strong>Stop the agent or scheduled job.</strong> Disable the MCP server entry or disconnect the client.</li> <li><strong>Lock 1Password.</strong> End the interactive SSH authorization session.</li> <li><strong>Remove the public key.</strong> Delete the test key from Bitbucket, the repository, or the remote account.</li> <li><strong>Revoke the service account.</strong> Remove its vault access and invalidate its token.</li> <li><strong>Delete the test SSH Key item</strong> after confirming no approved workflow uses the item.</li> <li><strong>Remove temporary configuration.</strong> Delete test references, local socket overrides, and generated logs.</li> <li><strong>Review evidence.</strong> Confirm the rollback record contains no private key, token, or environment dump.</li> </ol> <p><em>A deleted local file does not revoke a public key, service account, cached token, or remote authorization. Remove each grant at its source.</em></p> <h2 id="troubleshooting"> <a href="#troubleshooting" title="Troubleshooting">Troubleshooting</a> <a href="#troubleshooting" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Troubleshooting">#</a> </h2> <h3 id="the-agent-asks-for-a-key-on-every-command"> <a href="#the-agent-asks-for-a-key-on-every-command" title="The agent asks for a key on every command">The agent asks for a key on every command</a> <a href="#the-agent-asks-for-a-key-on-every-command" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The agent asks for a key on every command">#</a> </h3> <p>Check the selected authorization scope. Per-request approval is more restrictive. A terminal or application session might have ended. 1Password also asks again after a lock or quit event.</p> <h3 id="the-agent-sees-a-private-key-in-its-transcript"> <a href="#the-agent-sees-a-private-key-in-its-transcript" title="The agent sees a private key in its transcript">The agent sees a private key in its transcript</a> <a href="#the-agent-sees-a-private-key-in-its-transcript" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The agent sees a private key in its transcript">#</a> </h3> <p>Stop the workflow and rotate the key. Inspect the MCP server response, shell command, debug log, and tool wrapper. Replace private-key reads with SSH Agent use for interactive tasks. For jobs, replace a personal key with a dedicated identity and a documented exception.</p> <h3 id="a-key-list-contains-too-many-identities"> <a href="#a-key-list-contains-too-many-identities" title="A key list contains too many identities">A key list contains too many identities</a> <a href="#a-key-list-contains-too-many-identities" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A key list contains too many identities">#</a> </h3> <p>The 1Password SSH Agent exposes eligible keys from its configured vaults. Use a scoped agent configuration or host-specific SSH configuration. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="agent documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/agent"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/agent" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >agent documentation</a> </span> also notes the OpenSSH server six-key limit.</p> <h3 id="a-command-works-by-hand-but-fails-in-a-job"> <a href="#a-command-works-by-hand-but-fails-in-a-job" title="A command works by hand but fails in a job">A command works by hand but fails in a job</a> <a href="#a-command-works-by-hand-but-fails-in-a-job" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="A command works by hand but fails in a job">#</a> </h3> <p>Compare identity, vault scope, environment, host-key data, working directory, and approval assumptions. An interactive 1Password session includes human consent. A scheduled job does not. Design the job as a separate access mode.</p> <h3 id="the-mcp-server-is-connected-but-the-task-fails"> <a href="#the-mcp-server-is-connected-but-the-task-fails" title="The MCP server is connected but the task fails">The MCP server is connected but the task fails</a> <a href="#the-mcp-server-is-connected-but-the-task-fails" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The MCP server is connected but the task fails">#</a> </h3> <p>Connection does not prove authorization. Check tool discovery, server credentials, client consent, operating-system permissions, network access, and target-side permissions in separate steps. Keep the first test read-only.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Use the current 2026-07-28 MCP specification for new approvals. Any 2025-06-18 specification link in this article is historical background.</p> <p>Start with one synthetic repository and one read-only MCP tool. Record each expected result as untested until a controlled environment produces evidence. Then repeat the workflow with a non-production target, a named operator, a verified host key, and a written rollback record.</p> <p>Read the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password CLI reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/cli/reference"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/cli/reference" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password CLI reference</a> </span> for current command flags. Read <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Load secrets into scripts"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/cli/secrets-scripts"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/cli/secrets-scripts" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Load secrets into scripts</a> </span> before creating service-account automation. Read the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MCP specification"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28"> <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MCP specification</a> </span> before approving tools from a new server.</p> <p><strong>Keep interactive SSH human-approved. Keep unattended access separate. Keep private keys unread whenever the target supports agent-based authentication.</strong></p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Bitbucket Cloud SSH Keys: Read-Only Git Access for AI Agents
item.description: Set up Bitbucket Cloud SSH keys, Git CLI access, REST API tokens, 1Password, and MCP tools for read-only AI agent workflows.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>A bounded agent workflow separates repository reads, API reads, secret handling, and remote writes.</strong> Use Git over Secure Shell (SSH) for source access, a read-only Bitbucket access key for automated checkout, the REST API for metadata, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for approved tools. Store private keys and API tokens in 1Password. Keep writes behind a human approval step.</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Read-only default:</strong> Use a repository or project access key for agent checkout. Neither grants push access.</li> <li><strong>Personal identity:</strong> Use a personal SSH key for interactive work tied to a user account.</li> <li><strong>Secret custody:</strong> Use the 1Password SSH Agent so Git receives a signing operation without reading the private key.</li> <li><strong>CLI meaning:</strong> Treat <code>git</code>, <code>curl</code>, and a small audited API wrapper as the practical Bitbucket command line.</li> <li><strong>MCP boundary:</strong> Expose narrow read tools. Keep write tools disabled or behind a separate approval path.</li> <li><strong>Write gate:</strong> Let an agent inspect, compare, and prepare a change. Require a human to approve a push, pull request, merge, or settings update.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p><strong>Prerequisites:</strong> Bitbucket Cloud access, Git, an OpenSSH client, 1Password 8, 1Password CLI, a signed-in CLI or approved service account, and an MCP host with server approval controls. Set aside 45 minutes. Difficulty is intermediate.</p> <p>Use a test repository for the first pass. Replace every placeholder in the examples. The commands below are untested examples. They do not represent a live Bitbucket account or repository.</p> <p><strong>Version posture:</strong> This article is design guidance, not a version-pinned runbook. Confirm the installed Git, OpenSSH, 1Password CLI, Teamwork Graph CLI, MCP host, and MCP server versions before testing. Configure the 1Password SSH Agent for the current operating system before using <code>ssh-add -l</code>.</p> <p><strong>Keep credentials out of shells, logs, URLs, Git remotes, and source files.</strong> Use placeholders such as <code><workspace></code>, <code><repository></code>, <code><api-token></code>, and <code><socket-path></code>. Do not paste a real private key into a terminal transcript.</p> <h2 id="choose-the-access-boundary"> <a href="#choose-the-access-boundary" title="Choose the Access Boundary">Choose the Access Boundary</a> <a href="#choose-the-access-boundary" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Choose the Access Boundary">#</a> </h2> <p>Bitbucket Cloud supports access keys at repository, project, and workspace levels. The scope changes the impact of a copied key. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="official access-key comparison"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/kb/difference-between-repository-project-and-workspace-access-keys/"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/kb/difference-between-repository-project-and-workspace-access-keys/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >official access-key comparison</a> </span> states the permission difference directly.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Access path</th> <th>Scope</th> <th style="text-align: right">Write ability</th> <th>Good fit</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Repository access key</strong></td> <td>One repository</td> <td style="text-align: right">No</td> <td>Default agent checkout</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Project access key</strong></td> <td>Repositories in one project</td> <td style="text-align: right">No</td> <td>Read-only jobs across a small repository group</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Workspace access key</strong></td> <td>Repositories in one workspace</td> <td style="text-align: right">Yes</td> <td>Controlled service automation with a separate write plan</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Personal SSH key</strong></td> <td>Repositories allowed for one user</td> <td style="text-align: right">Follows the user account</td> <td>Interactive administration</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>API token</strong></td> <td>User-based API scopes and account reach</td> <td style="text-align: right">Depends on scopes</td> <td>REST API reads, or a temporary write task</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Start with the smallest useful boundary.</strong> Pick a repository access key when one repository is enough. Pick a project key when several repositories share one project and read-only access fits. Treat a workspace access key as a write identity, not as a convenient default.</p> <p>Create and register the smallest key through the matching Bitbucket settings path:</p> <ol> <li>Open Repository settings, Access keys, and Add key for one repository. Paste the public key and keep the key read-only.</li> <li>Open Project settings, Access keys, and Add key when several repositories need one project-scoped read identity.</li> <li>Use a workspace access key only in a shared workspace with an approved write design. Personal workspaces do not provide the same workspace-level path.</li> <li>Record the key label, scope, public-key fingerprint, owner, and rotation date. Keep the private key in 1Password.</li> </ol> <p>Run one exact read-only connection test after registration:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>git ls-remote git@bitbucket.org:<workspace>/<repository>.git HEAD </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Expected output:</strong> one commit reference for <code>HEAD</code>. Untested example. A successful result proves one permitted SSH identity reached the named repository. The result does not prove the registered key was selected or write access. Run the test again after the one-key-per-repository configuration.</p> <p>For private-key custody and 1Password SSH Agent consent, see <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password CLI and SSH Agent: Secure SSH Keys for AI Agents"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/1password-cli-ssh-keys-mcp-agent-administration/"> <a href="/articles/1password-cli-ssh-keys-mcp-agent-administration/" rel="follow me" >1Password CLI and SSH Agent: Secure SSH Keys for AI Agents</a> </span> .</p> <h2 id="define-bitbucket-cli-correctly"> <a href="#define-bitbucket-cli-correctly" title="Define “Bitbucket CLI” Correctly">Define “Bitbucket CLI” Correctly</a> <a href="#define-bitbucket-cli-correctly" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Define “Bitbucket CLI” Correctly">#</a> </h2> <p>The phrase <strong>Bitbucket CLI</strong> often mixes three different interfaces. Keep them separate.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Git CLI:</strong> <code>git clone</code> and <code>git fetch</code> move repository data over SSH or HTTPS. <code>git diff</code> compares local files or revisions.</li> <li><strong>REST client:</strong> <code>curl</code> or a reviewed wrapper calls the Bitbucket Cloud Representational State Transfer (REST) API. An API is a programmatic interface for requesting data or actions. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Bitbucket Cloud REST API reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/bitbucket/rest/"> <a href="https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/bitbucket/rest/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Bitbucket Cloud REST API reference</a> </span> lists repository, source, branch, pull request, pipeline, and status resources.</li> <li><strong>Atlassian CLI:</strong> <code>acli</code> is Atlassian’s official command line. Its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="introduction"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/acli/guides/introduction/"> <a href="https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/acli/guides/introduction/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >introduction</a> </span> describes the product, while its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="command reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/acli/reference/commands/"> <a href="https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/acli/reference/commands/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >command reference</a> </span> lists <code>admin</code>, <code>jira</code>, <code>feedback</code>, and <code>rovodev</code> surfaces. The reference does not document Bitbucket Cloud commands.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Atlassian’s official <code>acli</code> command reference does not document Bitbucket Cloud commands.</strong> Do not invent a command such as <code>acli bitbucket clone</code>. Use Git for Git operations and the REST API for Bitbucket Cloud data.</p> <h3 id="optional-teamwork-graph-cli"> <a href="#optional-teamwork-graph-cli" title="Optional Teamwork Graph CLI">Optional Teamwork Graph CLI</a> <a href="#optional-teamwork-graph-cli" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Optional Teamwork Graph CLI">#</a> </h3> <p><strong>Atlassian also publishes the Teamwork Graph CLI, or <code>twg</code>.</strong> Its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/twg-cli/"> <a href="https://developer.atlassian.com/cloud/twg-cli/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >overview</a> </span> and <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="command catalog"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://developer.atlassian.com/platform/teamwork-graph/twg-cli/commands/commands-catalog/"> <a href="https://developer.atlassian.com/platform/teamwork-graph/twg-cli/commands/commands-catalog/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >command catalog</a> </span> document Bitbucket command families. The setup command is:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>twg setup </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The setup command changes local authentication state. Follow the installed version’s prompts for optional Bitbucket token configuration. The CLI’s Bitbucket token path is separate from Atlassian OAuth. Keep exact command syntax tied to the installed version and current command catalog. Use a separate profile, a restricted token, reviewed installed skills, and human approval for mutating commands.</p> <p><strong>Expected result, untested:</strong> The isolated profile receives Bitbucket authentication settings. Record the previous profile state before setup. Remove the saved credential through the installed version’s documented logout or configuration-removal procedure during rollback.</p> <p>If a third-party project calls itself a Bitbucket CLI, audit its source, release process, checksums, update path, authentication flow, requested scopes, network destinations, log handling, and write commands. A familiar binary name does not establish vendor support or safe permissions.</p> <h2 id="keep-ssh-keys-under-1password-control"> <a href="#keep-ssh-keys-under-1password-control" title="Keep SSH Keys Under 1Password Control">Keep SSH Keys Under 1Password Control</a> <a href="#keep-ssh-keys-under-1password-control" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Keep SSH Keys Under 1Password Control">#</a> </h2> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password SSH Agent"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/agent"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/agent" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password SSH Agent</a> </span> offers SSH keys stored in 1Password to Git and SSH clients. The client performs an authorized signing request. The private key stays inside the 1Password app, and 1Password asks for consent before an approved client uses a key.</p> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password CLI reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/cli/reference"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/cli/reference" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password CLI reference</a> </span> serves a different role. Use <code>op</code> for controlled access to items, API tokens, service accounts, and automation setup. Use the SSH Agent for SSH signing. Avoid exporting a private key to a temporary file only to make an agent workflow easier.</p> <p>Check the local CLI and agent state with read-only commands:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>op --version </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>ssh-add -l </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Expected output:</strong> a 1Password CLI version and one or more public-key fingerprints from the active agent. Untested example. An empty <code>ssh-add -l</code> result means no key is available through the selected agent socket.</p> <p>For a new key, create an Ed25519 SSH Key item in 1Password or import one generated with a trusted local process. Set a label based on purpose, scope, and rotation date. Add only the public key to Bitbucket Cloud. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Linux repository access-key guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/set-up-repository-access-keys-on-linux/"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/set-up-repository-access-keys-on-linux/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Linux repository access-key guide</a> </span> describes the repository settings path and the read-only limitation.</p> <h2 id="verify-bitbuckets-host-key-first"> <a href="#verify-bitbuckets-host-key-first" title="Verify Bitbucket’s Host Key First">Verify Bitbucket’s Host Key First</a> <a href="#verify-bitbuckets-host-key-first" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Verify Bitbucket’s Host Key First">#</a> </h2> <p>SSH user authentication does not prove server identity. The client must verify Bitbucket Cloud’s host key before sending an authentication request. Atlassian’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="SSH and two-step verification guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/configure-ssh-and-two-step-verification/"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/configure-ssh-and-two-step-verification/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >SSH and two-step verification guide</a> </span> lists the public host keys and shows the official endpoint for retrieving known-host entries.</p> <p>Fetch the public host-key data for comparison:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>curl --fail --silent --show-error https://bitbucket.org/site/ssh </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Expected output:</strong> OpenSSH <code>known_hosts</code> lines for <code>bitbucket.org</code>. Untested example. Compare the returned key or fingerprint with an independent trusted copy before placing the line in <code>~/.ssh/known_hosts</code>.</p> <p>Use strict host checking after the approved entry exists:</p> <pre tabindex="0"><code class="language-sshconfig" data-lang="sshconfig">Host bitbucket.org StrictHostKeyChecking yes UserKnownHostsFile ~/.ssh/known_hosts </code></pre><p><strong>Do not accept a changed host key during an agent run.</strong> Stop the run, verify the current Bitbucket Cloud host-key record, and review the local <code>known_hosts</code> entry. An automatic acceptance step removes a key security boundary.</p> <h2 id="select-one-key-per-repository"> <a href="#select-one-key-per-repository" title="Select One Key Per Repository">Select One Key Per Repository</a> <a href="#select-one-key-per-repository" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Select One Key Per Repository">#</a> </h2> <p>One device often holds several Bitbucket keys. A broad SSH agent offers several identities during one connection. A server or policy with a small authentication-attempt limit might reject the right key after earlier keys fail.</p> <p>Atlassian’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="multiple repository access-key guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/managing-multiple-repository-access-keys-on-one-device/"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/managing-multiple-repository-access-keys-on-one-device/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >multiple repository access-key guide</a> </span> uses <code>core.sshCommand</code> inside a repository Git configuration file and <code>includeIf</code> in the global Git configuration. Follow the same pattern for one key per repository.</p> <p>Portable file-backed example:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-ini" data-lang="ini"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># .gitconfig inside one local repository</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#66d9ef">[core]</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#a6e22e">sshCommand</span> <span style="color:#f92672">=</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">ssh -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -i ~/.ssh/<repository-automation-key></span> </span></span></code></pre></div><div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-ini" data-lang="ini"><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#75715e"># ~/.gitconfig</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#66d9ef">[includeIf "gitdir:~/src/<repository>/"]</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span> <span style="color:#a6e22e">path</span> <span style="color:#f92672">=</span> <span style="color:#e6db74">~/src/<repository>/.gitconfig</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The block above is a file-backed private-key exception for a dedicated automation identity. The block does not configure the 1Password SSH Agent. For the 1Password SSH Agent, configure the platform-specific <code>IdentityAgent</code> or <code>SSH_AUTH_SOCK</code> value from the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="1Password setup guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/get-started"> <a href="https://www.1password.dev/ssh/get-started" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >1Password setup guide</a> </span> . Some OpenSSH configurations use a <code>.pub</code> file as an agent identity selector. Confirm platform support before using one. A file-backed setup needs the matching private-key path. Never pass a <code>.pub</code> file to a command expecting private-key material or export a personal private key.</p> <p>Use explicit repository configuration when a local clone needs one key. Use <code>includeIf</code> when a directory contains several clones sharing one access boundary. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="multiple-key guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/managing-multiple-repository-access-keys-on-one-device/"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/managing-multiple-repository-access-keys-on-one-device/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >multiple-key guide</a> </span> shows both settings in the Bitbucket workflow.</p> <p>Clone through Git over SSH:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>git clone git@bitbucket.org:<workspace>/<repository>.git <local-directory> </span></span></code></pre></div><p><strong>Expected output:</strong> Git creates <code><local-directory></code> and fetches the repository through <code>bitbucket.org</code>. Untested example. A repository access key permits clone and pull only.</p> <h2 id="use-api-tokens-for-narrow-rest-reads"> <a href="#use-api-tokens-for-narrow-rest-reads" title="Use API Tokens for Narrow REST Reads">Use API Tokens for Narrow REST Reads</a> <a href="#use-api-tokens-for-narrow-rest-reads" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Use API Tokens for Narrow REST Reads">#</a> </h2> <p>Use SSH for Git transport. Use the REST API for metadata or operations outside Git transport. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="API token permissions guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/api-token-permissions/"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/api-token-permissions/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >API token permissions guide</a> </span> lists repository scopes such as Read, Write, Admin, and Delete. Repository Read maps to <code>read:repository:bitbucket</code> and does not include pull request access.</p> <p>Prefer a Bitbucket repository or project access token for read automation when the target supports the required endpoint. A user-based API token retains the user account’s wider reach. Use a workspace access token only when the task record names the wider boundary. Review the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Bitbucket access-token guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/access-tokens/"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/access-tokens/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Bitbucket access-token guide</a> </span> before selecting the token type.</p> <p>For an agent read path, start with <code>read:repository:bitbucket</code>. Add <code>read:pullrequest:bitbucket</code> only when the agent needs pull request data. Add workspace or pipeline scopes only after the task record names the endpoint and result. Write and admin scopes need a separate approval path.</p> <p>Create each API token for one purpose, set an expiry date, store the expiry in the rotation record, and replace the token before expiry. Atlassian’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="API token creation guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/create-an-api-token/"> <a href="https://support.atlassian.com/bitbucket-cloud/docs/create-an-api-token/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >API token creation guide</a> </span> requires a name, expiry date, app selection, and scopes. The token appears once after creation.</p> <p>Keep the value in 1Password or a managed runtime secret. Do not put the value in a remote URL. Send a bearer token through an environment variable only inside the process needing one read:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>op run --env-file<span style="color:#f92672">=</span>/path/to/agent.env -- <span style="color:#ae81ff">\ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>sh -c <span style="color:#e6db74">'curl --fail --silent --show-error \ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> --request GET \ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> --url "https://api.bitbucket.org/2.0/repositories/<workspace>/<repository>" \ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> --header "Authorization: Bearer ${BITBUCKET_API_TOKEN}" \ </span></span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span><span style="color:#e6db74"> --header "Accept: application/json"'</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Keep <code>/path/to/agent.env</code> outside the repository. Store a reference such as <code>BITBUCKET_API_TOKEN=op://synthetic-vault/synthetic-api-token/credential</code> in the file. <code>op run</code> resolves the reference and exposes the value to the curl child process for the subprocess lifetime. It does not prevent the child process from reading or logging the environment value. Do not replace the placeholder with a literal token.</p> <p><strong>Expected output:</strong> JSON metadata for the selected repository. Untested example. The placeholder must never become a real token in a committed file or log.</p> <p>For longer automation, let 1Password inject a secret into the process environment through the supported CLI or service-account flow. Keep the token lifetime short enough for the task. Revoke a token when the task ends early or the host changes ownership.</p> <h2 id="give-mcp-a-small-read-surface"> <a href="#give-mcp-a-small-read-surface" title="Give MCP a Small Read Surface">Give MCP a Small Read Surface</a> <a href="#give-mcp-a-small-read-surface" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Give MCP a Small Read Surface">#</a> </h2> <p>Use the current <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MCP specification"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28"> <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MCP specification</a> </span> and its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="authorization rules"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization"> <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >authorization rules</a> </span> when reviewing a new server. HTTP servers need token audience checks and clear handling for 401 and 403 responses.</p> <p>The MCP host obtains user consent. The client maintains a connection to one server. The server exposes tools, resources, or prompts. Treat each server as untrusted code until its source, transport, account, and permissions pass review.</p> <p>The 2025-06-18 specification URL in the next paragraph is a historical version. Use the current 2026-07-28 specification for new reviews.</p> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="MCP specification"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18"> <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >MCP specification</a> </span> defines communication between an MCP host, client, and server. A server exposes tools, resources, or prompts through the protocol. MCP standardizes the connection format. The host, server implementation, account, token scope, and approval policy still decide what a call reaches.</p> <p>Use an MCP server as a narrow adapter over Git and the Bitbucket Cloud REST API.</p> <p>Protect this adapter against token passthrough, server-side request forgery (SSRF), and confused-deputy behavior. SSRF lets a server send requests to unintended destinations. Confused-deputy behavior occurs when a server uses broader privileges on behalf of a caller. Also protect against malicious local servers, unsafe OAuth redirects, and oversized source-data returns. Fix allowed Bitbucket origins and repository identifiers. Run local servers in a sandbox with a dedicated operating-system user. Redact secrets from tool results and logs.</p> <p>This section describes a design, not a tested MCP configuration. No client, server, transport, version, or fixture is pinned here. Validate one read-only server in a separate test profile before connecting an agent to a production repository.</p> <p>Example read tools include:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Tool</th> <th>Bounded result</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong><code>get_repository_metadata</code></strong></td> <td>Return one repository’s metadata</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>read_source_file</code></strong></td> <td>Read one path at one revision</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>list_branches</code></strong></td> <td>List branches for one repository</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>get_pull_request</code></strong></td> <td>Return one pull request after the token has pull request read scope</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong><code>get_build_status</code></strong></td> <td>Return status data for one commit</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>These names describe a design. They are not Atlassian command names. Keep the server from accepting arbitrary URLs, arbitrary shell commands, raw tokens, private-key export requests, or unrestricted repository identifiers.</p> <p>Set permissions at four layers:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Bitbucket Cloud:</strong> repository or project read key for Git, plus the smallest API token scopes for REST reads.</li> <li><strong>1Password:</strong> one vault or service account for the task, with no private-key export path.</li> <li><strong>MCP server:</strong> an allowlist of read tools, fixed Bitbucket Cloud endpoints, input validation, timeout limits, and redacted logs.</li> <li><strong>MCP host:</strong> user approval for the server and every write-capable action, with write tools disabled in the default profile.</li> </ol> <p><em>An MCP tool list proves discovery. The list does not prove authorization, correct scope, safe input handling, or a correct result.</em></p> <h2 id="stage-the-agent-workflow"> <a href="#stage-the-agent-workflow" title="Stage the Agent Workflow">Stage the Agent Workflow</a> <a href="#stage-the-agent-workflow" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Stage the Agent Workflow">#</a> </h2> <p>Keep the workflow explicit.
