The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox vzdump reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/vzdump.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/vzdump.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox <code>vzdump</code> reference</a> </span> documents the mode and storage options. Check the task log after the command returns. Do not treat an old backup as a current recovery point because its filename looks recent.</p> <p>If the target is <strong>PBS</strong>, run or inspect a verification job for the selected datastore. PBS <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="verification documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://pbs.proxmox.com/docs/maintenance.html"> <a href="https://pbs.proxmox.com/docs/maintenance.html" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >verification documentation</a> </span> explains how to verify backup data integrity and schedule repeated checks. Verification finds damaged backup chunks. <strong>A clean verification does not prove a restored operating system, application, or external dependency works.</strong> Continue with the restore drill even after a clean verification result.</p> <h2 id="restore-to-an-isolated-vm"> <a href="#restore-to-an-isolated-vm" title="Restore to an Isolated VM">Restore to an Isolated VM</a> <a href="#restore-to-an-isolated-vm" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Restore to an Isolated VM">#</a> </h2> <p>In the Proxmox interface, select the backup under the storage’s <strong>Backups</strong> view and choose <strong>Restore</strong>. Enter an unused VM ID and the intended target storage. Leave <strong>Start after restore</strong> off. Review the option for generating a new MAC address. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="official qmrestore synopsis"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/generated/qmrestore.1-synopsis.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/generated/qmrestore.1-synopsis.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >official <code>qmrestore</code> synopsis</a> </span> defines a unique VM ID, the storage choice, <code>--unique</code> for a random Ethernet address, and the default of not starting the restored VM.</p> <p>For a file-based <code>vzdump</code> archive, this shell command shows the equivalent pattern. Replace the archive path, new VM ID, and storage ID with values from your environment:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span style="display:flex;"><span>qmrestore /path/to/vzdump-qemu-120-2026_10_11-02_00_00.vma.zst <span style="color:#ae81ff">920</span> --storage local-lvm --unique <span style="color:#ae81ff">1</span> </span></span></code></pre></div><p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Proxmox restore description"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/qmrestore.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/qmrestore.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Proxmox restore description</a> </span> says a restore without a target storage tries the original storage. Set <strong><code>--storage</code></strong> when the old storage does not exist on the test node. Do not use <strong><code>--force</code></strong> for a drill. The option permits overwriting an existing VM, while this procedure requires an unused ID. PBS backups also restore through the Proxmox interface. Select the storage entry for the PBS snapshot rather than treating the snapshot as a local <code>.vma.zst</code> file.</p> <p>Before first boot, inspect every restored network interface, including secondary and passthrough interfaces. A <strong>MAC address</strong> identifies a network interface. <strong>DNS</strong> maps names to addresses. <strong>DHCP</strong> assigns network settings. A <strong>VLAN</strong> is a logical network carried over shared hardware. A <strong>virtual TPM</strong> stores security state for a guest. Disconnect every interface or connect every interface only to an isolated test segment. Confirm no production route, DNS path, DHCP service, management network, or external integration remains reachable. If the workload needs another test service, provide a test copy on the isolated network. Compare disk mappings, firmware, virtual TPM requirements, and any special devices with the source. External disks, passed-through devices, and secrets stored outside the VM need separate plans.</p> <h2 id="test-the-guest-and-workload"> <a href="#test-the-guest-and-workload" title="Test the Guest and Workload">Test the Guest and Workload</a> <a href="#test-the-guest-and-workload" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test the Guest and Workload">#</a> </h2> <p>Start the restored VM and use its console first. Confirm the operating system boots, all expected volumes mount, the clock is sane, and the application starts. Then run the pass condition written earlier. Compare a known data item with its pre-backup value and timestamp. A login prompt or running process alone does not show the service holds the right data.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Test</th> <th>Pass condition</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Boot</strong></td> <td>Guest reaches a normal login without repair mode or repeated recovery prompts.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Disks</strong></td> <td>Every disk included in the backup appears, mounts, and holds expected data.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Service</strong></td> <td>A representative local request or read succeeds.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Recovery point</strong></td> <td>The restored data meets the recorded RPO.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Recovery time</strong></td> <td>Restore plus boot and service validation meets the recorded RTO.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Isolation</strong></td> <td>No production address, job, or integration receives duplicate traffic.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Keep the restored guest isolated while you inspect scheduled tasks, notification hooks, backup agents, and application credentials. Do not run a test sending live customer messages or writing to production services. If a check fails, record the exact stage. Separate <strong>backup integrity failure</strong>, <strong>VM boot failure</strong>, <strong>missing data</strong>, and <strong>application failure</strong>. Each points to a different repair.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Failure class</th> <th>Confirming evidence</th> <th>First correction</th> <th>Retest</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Backup integrity</strong></td> <td>Verification or restore task reports damaged data</td> <td>Select another verified recovery point and inspect storage health</td> <td>Repeat verification and restore</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>VM boot</strong></td> <td>Console shows firmware, disk, or recovery errors</td> <td>Compare firmware, disk mapping, and boot order with the source</td> <td>Boot the isolated copy and record the console result</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Missing data</strong></td> <td>Expected file, volume, or database record is absent</td> <td>Check excluded disks, mounts, snapshots, and external dependencies</td> <td>Repeat the named file or data check</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Application</strong></td> <td>Guest boots but the service check fails</td> <td>Inspect service logs, credentials, dependencies, and recovery steps</td> <td>Run the same local health check and workload test</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Proxmox offers <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="single-file restore for PBS backups"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/vzdump.adoc"> <a href="https://github.com/proxmox/pve-docs/blob/master/vzdump.adoc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >single-file restore for PBS backups</a> </span> . Use single-file restore to test a file recovery path when your workload needs one. A recovered file still does not replace a full VM boot and service test. Proxmox also offers live restore from PBS. Its documentation says a failed live restore leaves the VM in an undefined state, so use the normal completed restore for this planned drill.</p> <h2 id="record-the-result-and-close-the-drill"> <a href="#record-the-result-and-close-the-drill" title="Record the Result and Close the Drill">Record the Result and Close the Drill</a> <a href="#record-the-result-and-close-the-drill" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Record the Result and Close the Drill">#</a> </h2> <p>Record the source VM ID, backup storage, backup timestamp, backup mode, new VM ID, target storage, network isolation, restore start and finish times, application test, data timestamp, and any failed checks. Compare the measured recovery point and time with your targets. A failure is useful evidence only if you change the backup plan and repeat the drill.</p> <p>Shut down the restored VM when testing ends. Remove its test copy only after saving the result, and verify the production VM still runs as expected. Keep the backup under your normal retention policy. Do not change retention merely to make one drill pass.</p> <p>Repeat the test after major storage, guest, or backup configuration changes. Rotate through important VMs, including guests with excluded disks or external dependencies. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Hyper-V to Proxmox migration guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/hyper-v-to-proxmox-migration-checklist/"> <a href="/articles/hyper-v-to-proxmox-migration-checklist/" rel="follow me" >Hyper-V to Proxmox migration guide</a> </span> uses this recovery proof before retiring a source VM. <strong>A usable backup has a known restore path, a tested workload, and a measured recovery point.</strong></p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Repeat the drill after storage, guest, or backup changes. Review the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="homelab backup restore drill"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/homelab-backup-restore-drill/"> <a href="/articles/homelab-backup-restore-drill/" rel="follow me" >homelab backup restore drill</a> </span> for file-level recovery.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Secure AI Agents and MCP Capstone Answer Key
item.description: Compare a completed Secure AI Agents and MCP capstone with the reference deployment decision and required security conditions.
item.content:encoded: <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Return to the Secure AI Agents and MCP Capstone"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/secure-ai-agents-mcp-course/06-capstone/"> <a href="/secure-ai-agents-mcp-course/06-capstone/" rel="follow me" >Return to the Secure AI Agents and MCP Capstone</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Open this reference after you finish and score your capstone package.</strong> Record each difference as a correction or residual risk.</p> <h2 id="reference-decision"> <a href="#reference-decision" title="Reference Decision">Reference Decision</a> <a href="#reference-decision" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Reference Decision">#</a> </h2> <p>The reference decision is <strong>approve with conditions for a test environment</strong>.</p> <p>Required conditions:</p> <ol> <li><code>post_comment</code> uses a dedicated test-project identity.</li> <li>The host shows the issue identifier and final comment text.</li> <li>A trusted host records approval with a random, single-use token bound to the action digest and expiry. Untrusted content cannot mint approval.</li> <li>The server rejects any other project, issue, or payload over 2,000 characters. Approval binds the preview and current target-state digest.</li> <li>The event stream records preview, approval, call, and downstream result under one run ID.</li> <li>A hostile issue instruction fails before the downstream request.</li> <li>A valid approved comment returns <code>would_post</code> in the synthetic positive test. The local simulator prints <code>9/9 passed</code> and makes no downstream request.</li> </ol> <p>Production release stays out of scope until a real authorization test, downstream audit review, and incident exercise produce evidence.</p> <h2 id="review-gate"> <a href="#review-gate" title="Review Gate">Review Gate</a> <a href="#review-gate" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Review Gate">#</a> </h2> <p>Use the rubric on the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="capstone prompt"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/secure-ai-agents-mcp-course/06-capstone/"> <a href="/secure-ai-agents-mcp-course/06-capstone/" rel="follow me" >capstone prompt</a> </span> . Pass when the package scores <strong>10 out of 12 or higher</strong> and authority, approval, and attack test each score at least one point.</p> <h2 id="verify-your-review"> <a href="#verify-your-review" title="Verify Your Review">Verify Your Review</a> <a href="#verify-your-review" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Verify Your Review">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><input disabled="" type="checkbox"> The decision names the test-only release boundary</li> <li><input disabled="" type="checkbox"> All seven required conditions appear in the package or correction record</li> <li><input disabled="" type="checkbox"> The score reaches 10 out of 12</li> <li><input disabled="" type="checkbox"> Authority, approval, and attack test have no zero scores</li> <li><input disabled="" type="checkbox"> Production evidence gaps have owners and follow-up checks</li> </ul> <p>Return to the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Secure AI Agents and MCP Course"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/secure-ai-agents-mcp-course-start/"> <a href="/secure-ai-agents-mcp-course-start/" rel="follow me" >Secure AI Agents and MCP Course</a> </span> after you record corrections and the final score.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Secure AI Agents and MCP Quiz Answer Key
item.description: Score the Secure AI Agents and MCP knowledge check, review each reason, and repair missed security artifacts before the capstone.
item.content:encoded: <p> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Return to the Secure AI Agents and MCP Quiz"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/secure-ai-agents-mcp-course/05-knowledge-check/"> <a href="/secure-ai-agents-mcp-course/05-knowledge-check/" rel="follow me" >Return to the Secure AI Agents and MCP Quiz</a> </span> </p> <p><strong>Use this key after you answer all ten questions.</strong> Compare your reason with the security boundary or evidence named below.</p> <h2 id="answer-key"> <a href="#answer-key" title="Answer Key">Answer Key</a> <a href="#answer-key" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Answer Key">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>#</th> <th>Answer</th> <th>Reason</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>1</strong></td> <td>C</td> <td>Enforcement belongs outside untrusted content and model output.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>2</strong></td> <td>C</td> <td>The server validates a trusted host-held, single-use approval token and bound target state before the narrow write. A caller-supplied digest does not prove approval.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>3</strong></td> <td>B</td> <td>Schema validates shape. Server logic and identity controls enforce authority.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>4</strong></td> <td>B</td> <td>Approval needs the final action, target, payload, and effect.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>5</strong></td> <td>C</td> <td>An independent enforcement event proves the decision with useful context.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>6</strong></td> <td>B</td> <td>Environment inheritance often carries credentials and host configuration.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>7</strong></td> <td>A</td> <td>Tokens need audience and boundary checks. A token for one service should not flow to another.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>8</strong></td> <td>B</td> <td>The host should stop after the defined repeated failure threshold.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>9</strong></td> <td>C</td> <td>A controlled retest proves the enforcement change addresses the observed path.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>10</strong></td> <td>B</td> <td>Security review follows behavior and authority, not the feature label.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="passing-gate"> <a href="#passing-gate" title="Passing Gate">Passing Gate</a> <a href="#passing-gate" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Passing Gate">#</a> </h2> <p>You pass when your score reaches <strong>8 out of 10</strong> and questions <strong>1, 2, 4, and 5</strong> are correct.</p> <ul> <li><strong>Pass both gates:</strong> Record your score and start the capstone.</li> <li><strong>Miss a core question:</strong> Revisit the related lesson, repair the artifact, and answer the question again.</li> <li><strong>Score below eight:</strong> Review every missed topic, update the related artifacts, and retake the quiz from a clean copy.</li> </ul> <h2 id="verify-your-review"> <a href="#verify-your-review" title="Verify Your Review">Verify Your Review</a> <a href="#verify-your-review" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Verify Your Review">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><input disabled="" type="checkbox"> The recorded score reaches 8 out of 10</li> <li><input disabled="" type="checkbox"> Questions 1, 2, 4, and 5 are correct</li> <li><input disabled="" type="checkbox"> Every missed answer has a corrected reason</li> <li><input disabled="" type="checkbox"> Every related course artifact reflects the correction</li> </ul> <p>Continue with the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Security Capstone"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/secure-ai-agents-mcp-course/06-capstone/"> <a href="/secure-ai-agents-mcp-course/06-capstone/" rel="follow me" >Security Capstone</a> </span> after you pass both gates.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Test Browser DNS and WebRTC Leaks With a VPN
item.description: Check your browser's public IP, DNS resolver, and WebRTC addresses before and after connecting a VPN. Interpret results and isolate routing problems.
item.content:encoded: <p>A virtual private network (VPN) connection icon does not prove every browser request follows the same route. Test your <strong>public IP</strong>, <strong>Domain Name System (DNS) resolver</strong>, and <strong>WebRTC addresses</strong> separately. Each result answers a different question. This guide gives you a repeatable check and a way to investigate an unexpected result.</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Compare two states:</strong> Record the same tests before and after connecting your VPN.</li> <li><strong>Read each result separately:</strong> A changed public IP does not establish where DNS queries went.</li> <li><strong>Check WebRTC candidates:</strong> Look for a public address from outside your intended route. A private address has a different meaning.</li> <li><strong>Change one setting:</strong> Retest after each VPN, browser, or DNS adjustment.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p>Use the browser and network connection you intend to protect. Know whether your VPN should cover the whole device or only selected apps. If your VPN uses split tunneling, record whether the test browser belongs inside the tunnel. Keep the VPN client’s DNS policy available for comparison.</p> <p><strong>Split tunneling</strong> sends selected apps through the VPN while other apps use the normal network.</p> <p>This procedure uses <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="BrowserLeaks IP"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://browserleaks.com/ip"> <a href="https://browserleaks.com/ip" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >BrowserLeaks IP</a> </span> , <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DNS"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://browserleaks.com/dns"> <a href="https://browserleaks.com/dns" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >DNS</a> </span> , and <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="WebRTC"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://browserleaks.com/webrtc"> <a href="https://browserleaks.com/webrtc" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >WebRTC</a> </span> pages. The service sees your connection address when you visit. Its DNS test asks the browser to resolve 50 random names, according to the test description. Avoid running an external test on a managed or restricted network without approval. Do not paste credentials, internal hostnames, or private browsing records into a test site.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Warning:</strong> Keep your exact IP addresses out of public screenshots and support posts. Record whether addresses match your expected ISP or VPN route. Share the actual values only through an approved support channel.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="know-what-each-test-shows"> <a href="#know-what-each-test-shows" title="Know What Each Test Shows">Know What Each Test Shows</a> <a href="#know-what-each-test-shows" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Know What Each Test Shows">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Check</th> <th>What to compare</th> <th>What the result does not prove</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Public IP</strong></td> <td>Address seen by an ordinary website</td> <td>Which resolver handled DNS</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>DNS resolver</strong></td> <td>Servers observed during new name lookups</td> <td>Where every app sends DNS</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>WebRTC</strong></td> <td>Local and public connection candidates</td> <td>Which candidate a later call uses</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The public IP page reports the address used for its web request. The DNS page triggers new lookups and reports the resolvers serving them. WebRTC, short for Web Real-Time Communication, lets browser applications establish peer connections. The WebRTC page checks addresses exposed during those connections. An <strong>ICE candidate</strong> is a possible network address for a peer connection. A <strong>VPN exit</strong> is the public address used after traffic leaves the VPN. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="RFC 8828"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8828"> <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8828" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >RFC 8828</a> </span> explains why WebRTC’s connection candidates sometimes contain addresses beyond the one seen by an ordinary web request, especially with split tunnels or proxies.</p> <p>A DNS server owned by your VPN provider, a separate resolver selected inside the VPN, or a browser-selected encrypted resolver all produce different names in a test. A resolver name alone does not identify a leak. Compare the name with the policy you intended to use.</p> <h2 id="record-a-baseline"> <a href="#record-a-baseline" title="Record a Baseline">Record a Baseline</a> <a href="#record-a-baseline" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Record a Baseline">#</a> </h2> <p>Disconnect the VPN only if your situation permits an untunneled baseline. Open the three test pages in one normal browser profile. Run the DNS test and wait for the result. Record the following without publishing exact addresses:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Field</th> <th>Baseline note</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Browser and version</strong></td> <td>Name, version, and relevant privacy extensions</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Network</strong></td> <td>Home Wi-Fi, mobile hotspot, or another approved network</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Public IPv4 and IPv6</strong></td> <td>Whether each belongs to your ordinary connection</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>DNS result</strong></td> <td>Resolver names or operators shown</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>WebRTC result</strong></td> <td>Public, private, or <code>.local</code> candidates shown</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>If you cannot disconnect the VPN, start with the expected VPN route and mark the untunneled baseline as unavailable. Do not infer your ordinary ISP address from a location label or a map. Location databases sometimes differ from the actual network operator.</p> <h2 id="repeat-with-the-vpn-connected"> <a href="#repeat-with-the-vpn-connected" title="Repeat With the VPN Connected">Repeat With the VPN Connected</a> <a href="#repeat-with-the-vpn-connected" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Repeat With the VPN Connected">#</a> </h2> <p>Connect the VPN and confirm the client reports a working tunnel. Reload each test page in the <strong>same browser profile</strong>. Run the DNS test again to create fresh lookups. Record both IPv4 and IPv6 results when the service reports them.</p> <p>Compare the results in this order:</p> <ol> <li><strong>Public IP:</strong> The web request should show an address consistent with the VPN exit or the route you deliberately configured. An unchanged ordinary ISP address is a routing problem if the browser should be inside the tunnel.</li> <li><strong>DNS:</strong> Compare each reported resolver with your VPN and browser DNS settings. An ISP resolver outside the intended tunnel deserves investigation. A named third-party resolver is expected if you deliberately selected the resolver in the browser.</li> <li><strong>WebRTC:</strong> Compare the public WebRTC candidate with the VPN exit and the baseline public IP. A baseline ISP public address appearing only in WebRTC is a concern when all browser traffic should use the VPN.</li> <li><strong>Private addresses:</strong> An address in the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="RFC 1918 private ranges"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918"> <a href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >RFC 1918 private ranges</a> </span> , or a <code>.local</code> candidate, differs from a public ISP address. Record the local entry and decide whether the site should learn the address.</li> </ol> <p>The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="WebRTC IP handling standard"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8828"> <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8828" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >WebRTC IP handling standard</a> </span> describes how an app learns additional public or private addresses through ICE candidate discovery. Chromium’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="mDNS host candidate design"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/z5hSy6Rf_aE/m/aGND030cAgAJ"> <a href="https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/z5hSy6Rf_aE/m/aGND030cAgAJ" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >mDNS host candidate design</a> </span> replaces some private addresses with <code>.local</code> names. A blank WebRTC result is <strong>inconclusive</strong> if JavaScript, the API, or the test server did not work. A blank result does not prove complete protection.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Expected Result:</strong> Your browser’s ordinary web request and public WebRTC candidates follow the route you chose. DNS results match the VPN or browser resolver policy you recorded.</p> </blockquote> <h2 id="investigate-a-dns-mismatch"> <a href="#investigate-a-dns-mismatch" title="Investigate a DNS Mismatch">Investigate a DNS Mismatch</a> <a href="#investigate-a-dns-mismatch" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Investigate a DNS Mismatch">#</a> </h2> <p>First check whether the browser chooses its own resolver. Firefox’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DNS over HTTPS settings"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/dns-over-https"> <a href="https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/dns-over-https" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >DNS over HTTPS settings</a> </span> show an active status and a protection level. Default protection falls back to the system resolver under some conditions and respects network signals. Increased and Custom protection use a selected provider with backup behavior. Max protection warns when secure resolution fails. The status and exception list matter more than a toggle alone.</p> <p>Chrome’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Secure DNS guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/10468685?co=GENIE.Platform%3DDesktop&hl=en"> <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/10468685?co=GENIE.Platform%3DDesktop&hl=en" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Secure DNS guide</a> </span> describes automatic mode and a custom provider. Automatic mode falls back to an unencrypted lookup if secure lookup fails. A custom provider does not default to unencrypted mode. Managed devices and parental controls restrict this setting. Check the current browser UI before changing a managed policy.</p> <p>If the browser’s resolver is not the cause, compare the VPN client’s DNS setting, split-tunnel app list, operating system resolver, and IPv6 route. Change one item, then repeat the DNS test. A browser DNS test measures the tested browser’s lookup path. The result does not establish how another app resolves names. If your network uses <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DNS filtering"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/nextdns-vs-adguard-ad-blocker-comparison/"> <a href="/articles/nextdns-vs-adguard-ad-blocker-comparison/" rel="follow me" >DNS filtering</a> </span> , test one domain you intentionally block and one you allow. Do not treat a missing advertisement as proof of resolver routing.</p> <h2 id="investigate-a-webrtc-mismatch"> <a href="#investigate-a-webrtc-mismatch" title="Investigate a WebRTC Mismatch">Investigate a WebRTC Mismatch</a> <a href="#investigate-a-webrtc-mismatch" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Investigate a WebRTC Mismatch">#</a> </h2> <p>Check whether the browser is excluded from the VPN tunnel or uses a proxy outside the intended route. Test again after correcting the route. Do not disable IPv6 or WebRTC as a first response to a single ambiguous result. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="WebRTC standard"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8828"> <a href="https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8828" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >WebRTC standard</a> </span> describes a tradeoff between address exposure and direct call performance. Restricting candidates or forcing a proxy affects video calls and other peer connections.</p> <p>If your browser or VPN offers a documented WebRTC IP handling control, read its current description and choose a policy consistent with your use of calls. Retest the public candidate. A local address alone does not prove your ISP public address escaped the VPN. An exposed public ISP address, compared with a different VPN HTTP address, is the stronger signal.</p> <h2 id="keep-a-test-record"> <a href="#keep-a-test-record" title="Keep a Test Record">Keep a Test Record</a> <a href="#keep-a-test-record" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Keep a Test Record">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Field</th> <th>Result to enter</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Date and browser</strong></td> <td>Version, profile, extensions, and network</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Expected route</strong></td> <td>Whole-device VPN, split tunnel, or browser proxy</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Before and after</strong></td> <td>Public IP operator, DNS operator, WebRTC public candidate</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Mismatch</strong></td> <td>Which result disagreed with the intended policy</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Single change</strong></td> <td>Setting changed and the reason</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Retest</strong></td> <td>New result and any remaining uncertainty</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>Run the check again after browser, VPN, or network configuration changes. One clean result covers the tested browser, profile, network, and moment. A clean result does not establish anonymity or cover every app. If you are still choosing a browser, use the site’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="privacy browser comparison"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/best-privacy-browsers-librewolf-brave-firefox-tor/"> <a href="/articles/best-privacy-browsers-librewolf-brave-firefox-tor/" rel="follow me" >privacy browser comparison</a> </span> for features, then run this test on your own setup.</p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Repeat the test after browser, VPN, or network changes. Use the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="privacy browser comparison"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/best-privacy-browsers-librewolf-brave-firefox-tor/"> <a href="/articles/best-privacy-browsers-librewolf-brave-firefox-tor/" rel="follow me" >privacy browser comparison</a> </span> when choosing a browser.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Test Guest and IoT Isolation on a Mesh Wi-Fi Network
item.description: Verify whether your mesh guest and IoT networks block access to your home devices. Use a known working service, test each network, and record the limits.
item.content:encoded: <p>A separate Wi-Fi name does not reveal which devices communicate with each other. A mesh system might treat its <strong>guest network</strong>, <strong>IoT network</strong>, and <strong>wireless client isolation</strong> as different controls. This guide helps you test the paths on your own equipment without assuming a vendor’s label describes your policy.</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Prove the target works first:</strong> Reach a known service from your main network before testing a blocked path.</li> <li><strong>Test each boundary:</strong> Guest-to-main, IoT-to-main, and guest-to-guest access answer different questions.</li> <li><strong>Record the setup:</strong> Model, firmware, router or access-point mode, and connected mesh node affect interpretation.</li> <li><strong>Retest after changes:</strong> A clean result applies to the tested devices, service, address family, and configuration.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p>Allow about 20 minutes. You need a laptop able to join your main, guest, and IoT Wi-Fi networks. You also need a trusted device on the main network with a <strong>known open TCP service</strong>, such as a NAS web interface. A TCP service is a network service listening on a numbered port, such as a NAS web page on port 443. Use a service you own or administer. Note its local address and port without publishing them. Keep the service running throughout the test.</p> <p>Write down the mesh model, firmware version, operating mode, and the settings for guest access, IoT access, shared devices, and client isolation. Confirm the laptop’s Wi-Fi name after every switch. Disconnect a VPN or proxy for this local-path test if your normal policy permits the change, then restore the VPN or proxy afterward. A VPN changes the route under test.</p> <blockquote> <p><strong>Warning:</strong> Test only your own devices or devices you have permission to administer. A router’s login page is a poor substitute for a main-network host because gateway access follows separate rules.</p> </blockquote> <p>A <strong>local area network (LAN)</strong> is your private home network. <strong>IoT</strong>, or Internet of Things, includes devices such as cameras, speakers, and smart plugs. <strong>Client isolation</strong> blocks direct device-to-device traffic on one Wi-Fi network.</p> <h2 id="define-the-boundary"> <a href="#define-the-boundary" title="Define the Boundary">Define the Boundary</a> <a href="#define-the-boundary" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Define the Boundary">#</a> </h2> <p>Choose the result you want before changing a setting. Internet access and local access are separate outcomes.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Path</th> <th>Question to answer</th> <th>Example expected result</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Guest to main LAN</strong></td> <td>Reachability of a computer or NAS</td> <td>Blocked, unless you chose an exception</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>IoT to main LAN</strong></td> <td>Reachability of private devices</td> <td>Depends on the product and your policy</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guest to guest</strong></td> <td>Reachability between two guests</td> <td>Depends on client isolation settings</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guest to shared device</strong></td> <td>Use of a printer or display you shared</td> <td>Allowed only when intended</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guest to Internet</strong></td> <td>Access to an ordinary public site</td> <td>Allowed if your guest policy includes Internet</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>These rows are separate tests. TP-Link’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Deco device isolation guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/3968/"> <a href="https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/3968/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Deco device isolation guide</a> </span> says isolated devices retain Internet access and communication with other isolated devices, while access to main-network devices is blocked. ASUS’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="AP isolation guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.asus.com/us/support/faq/1044821/"> <a href="https://www.asus.com/us/support/faq/1044821/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >AP isolation guide</a> </span> describes a wireless peer control and notes a path through an upstream wired router falls outside the control. <strong>Do not treat one blocked path as proof of every other boundary.</strong></p> <h2 id="check-the-mesh-settings"> <a href="#check-the-mesh-settings" title="Check the Mesh Settings">Check the Mesh Settings</a> <a href="#check-the-mesh-settings" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check the Mesh Settings">#</a> </h2> <p>Find the feature controlling the boundary you plan to test. Menu names and availability vary with the model and firmware.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Mesh setting</th> <th>What to verify</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>TP-Link Deco guest network</strong></td> <td> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Router mode isolates guest from main"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/1460/"> <a href="https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/1460/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Router mode isolates guest from main</a> </span> . In access-point mode, check the <strong>Allow Local Access</strong> setting.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>ASUS guest profile</strong></td> <td> <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Access Intranet"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.asus.com/uk/support/faq/1009857/"> <a href="https://www.asus.com/uk/support/faq/1009857/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Access Intranet</a> </span> controls access to the main network on supported profiles.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Google Nest guest Wi-Fi</strong></td> <td>Check the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Shared devices"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.google.com/googlehome/answer/6327302?hl=en"> <a href="https://support.google.com/googlehome/answer/6327302?hl=en" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Shared devices</a> </span> list before expecting a printer or display to be hidden.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>IoT network or device isolation</strong></td> <td>Check whether the product offers a separate isolation control. An IoT Wi-Fi name alone does not establish the access rule.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>On Deco, <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="device isolation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/3968/"> <a href="https://www.tp-link.com/us/support/faq/3968/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >device isolation</a> </span> requires support from the main and satellite units. Record which node serves your test laptop. If a feature is absent, check the exact model and firmware documentation instead of assuming an app screen matches another owner’s setup.</p> <h2 id="establish-a-positive-control"> <a href="#establish-a-positive-control" title="Establish a Positive Control">Establish a Positive Control</a> <a href="#establish-a-positive-control" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Establish a Positive Control">#</a> </h2> <p>Connect the Windows test laptop to the <strong>main Wi-Fi</strong>. Confirm the chosen service works from this laptop. If you use PowerShell, enter the main-network host address and its known open port when prompted:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-powershell" data-lang="powershell"><span style="display:flex;"><span>$targetAddress = Read-Host <span style="color:#e6db74">"Main-network test host address"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>$targetPort = [<span style="color:#66d9ef">int</span>](Read-Host <span style="color:#e6db74">"Known open TCP port"</span>) </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Test-NetConnection -ComputerName $targetAddress -Port $targetPort </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Test-NetConnection documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/nettcpip/test-netconnection"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/nettcpip/test-netconnection" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Test-NetConnection documentation</a> </span> defines <code>-ComputerName</code> and <code>-Port</code> as a specific host and TCP service test. Record <code>TcpTestSucceeded</code>. Establish <code>True</code> here before interpreting a later <code>False</code>. A failed main-network test points to the service, address, host firewall, or laptop setup. Fix the main-network test first.</p> <p>If you use a phone or another operating system, open the same known service in its browser or app. Keep the exact service and target address the same when you switch Wi-Fi networks. A device-discovery list alone is weaker evidence because discovery traffic and direct TCP access follow different paths.</p> <h2 id="test-guest-and-iot-access"> <a href="#test-guest-and-iot-access" title="Test Guest and IoT Access">Test Guest and IoT Access</a> <a href="#test-guest-and-iot-access" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Test Guest and IoT Access">#</a> </h2> <p>Switch the same laptop to <strong>guest Wi-Fi</strong>. Confirm the Wi-Fi name. Load a public website if Internet access is part of your guest policy. Rerun the same <code>Test-NetConnection</code> command without changing <code>$targetAddress</code> or <code>$targetPort</code>. Record the result.</p> <p>Switch back to the main network and confirm the service still returns <code>True</code>. If the main-network test now fails, the guest failure is inconclusive. Then join the <strong>IoT Wi-Fi</strong> with the same laptop if your system permits a laptop connection and repeat the test. Do not assume the IoT result will match the guest result. A successful IoT-to-main test means the chosen local TCP service was reachable from the IoT network in this configuration.</p> <p>If you expect guests to be isolated from each other, use two devices you control on the guest network. Test a known service on one device from the other. Record this separately from guest-to-main access. If you expect a shared printer or display to work, test the intended exception as well. Cloud control of a smart device does not prove a direct local path.</p> <p>Repeat the guest-to-main test near each mesh node. Confirm the serving node in the app when the app reports one. <strong>IPv6</strong> is the newer Internet Protocol address family that uses 128-bit addresses. If the main host supports IPv6 and the main-network positive control succeeds over IPv6, repeat the same address-family test from guest and IoT Wi-Fi. An IPv4-only pass does not cover an IPv6 path.</p> <h2 id="interpret-a-mismatch"> <a href="#interpret-a-mismatch" title="Interpret a Mismatch">Interpret a Mismatch</a> <a href="#interpret-a-mismatch" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Interpret a Mismatch">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Observation</th> <th>Next check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Main and guest both fail</strong></td> <td>Check the target service, address, port, and host firewall. Isolation is unproven.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Main succeeds, guest succeeds</strong></td> <td>Check guest local-access settings, shared-device exceptions, and router versus access-point mode.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Main succeeds, guest fails</strong></td> <td>Record evidence for this target and TCP path. Test other paths required by your policy.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guest blocked, IoT succeeds</strong></td> <td>Check whether the IoT name is a compatibility network without a matching isolation rule.</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Guest-to-main blocked, guest-to-guest succeeds</strong></td> <td>Check wireless client isolation separately.</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>A failed <strong>ping</strong> does not settle the TCP question. A host firewall might block ping while accepting the service you chose. A failed TCP test is also narrow: the result says nothing about other ports, devices, IPv6, or shared-device exceptions. Treat a mismatch as a reason to check the configured rule and repeat a controlled test.</p> <h2 id="fix-and-record-the-result"> <a href="#fix-and-record-the-result" title="Fix and Record the Result">Fix and Record the Result</a> <a href="#fix-and-record-the-result" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Fix and Record the Result">#</a> </h2> <p>Change one control at a time. On a Deco in access-point mode, inspect <strong>Allow Local Access</strong>. On an ASUS guest profile, inspect <strong>Access Intranet</strong>. On Google Nest Wifi, remove an unintended item from <strong>Shared devices</strong>. If you need local smart-home control, decide which device must reach which service before adding an exception. A <strong>VLAN</strong> is a logical network carried over shared hardware. The site’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="VLAN segmentation plan"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/homelab-vlan-segmentation-plan/"> <a href="/articles/homelab-vlan-segmentation-plan/" rel="follow me" >VLAN segmentation plan</a> </span> covers a managed network when a consumer mesh lacks the access rule you need.</p> <p>Record the mesh model, firmware, operating mode, node, Wi-Fi network name, source device, destination service, address family, expected result, actual result, and the single change made. Do not publish private addresses or network passwords. Repeat the same tests after firmware updates, node changes, or a switch between router and access-point modes.</p> <p>If you are still choosing equipment, compare features in the site’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="mesh Wi-Fi buying guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/best-wifi-mesh-system-for-consumers/"> <a href="/articles/best-wifi-mesh-system-for-consumers/" rel="follow me" >mesh Wi-Fi buying guide</a> </span> . Then use this procedure to verify the network you install. <strong>A label or app toggle is a claim. A positive control and a matched retest give you evidence for the exact path you care about.</strong></p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Repeat the isolation tests after firmware, node, or operating-mode changes. Use the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="VLAN segmentation plan"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/homelab-vlan-segmentation-plan/"> <a href="/articles/homelab-vlan-segmentation-plan/" rel="follow me" >VLAN segmentation plan</a> </span> when mesh controls do not meet the required boundary.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: Why DNS Filtering Is Bypassed: Test the Resolver Path
item.description: Find why a device or browser skips your DNS filter. Compare direct and default queries, inspect logs, then check encrypted DNS, VPN, IPv6, and router settings.
item.content:encoded: <p>You configured a filtering resolver, yet one device still reaches a domain your policy blocks. The cause might be the rule, the device’s Domain Name System (DNS) assignment, a browser’s encrypted resolver, or a VPN. <strong>Test the path before changing settings.</strong> A direct query to the filter and an ordinary device query answer different questions.</p> <h2 id="key-takeaways"> <a href="#key-takeaways" title="Key Takeaways">Key Takeaways</a> <a href="#key-takeaways" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Key Takeaways">#</a> </h2> <ul> <li><strong>Check the rule first:</strong> Confirm the filter receives and blocks a safe test domain.</li> <li><strong>Trace each layer:</strong> Router, operating system, browser, VPN, and mobile settings each influence DNS routing.</li> <li><strong>Use fresh queries:</strong> Match a new hostname and timestamp with the filter’s query log.</li> <li><strong>State the limit:</strong> One observed query proves one path, not every app or device.</li> </ul> <h2 id="before-you-begin"> <a href="#before-you-begin" title="Before You Begin">Before You Begin</a> <a href="#before-you-begin" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Before You Begin">#</a> </h2> <p>Allow about 20 minutes. You need access to the filtering resolver’s query log, one device with the problem, and a record of the router’s DNS settings. Examples use a Windows laptop and <strong>Pi-hole</strong>, but the same comparison works with a resolver offering per-client query logs. Identify the exact filter address before starting. Do not paste private client addresses, query logs, or policy rules into a public report.</p> <p>Choose a <strong>harmless test domain</strong> already blocked by your policy. Another option is a temporary exact deny rule for a domain you control in a test profile. Record the rule and remove the rule after testing. Do not use a live malware domain as a probe. A blocked page is a useful symptom, but the resolver log supplies the stronger path evidence.</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Layer</th> <th>Question</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Filter</strong></td> <td>Does a direct query reach the intended resolver and match the rule?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Device</strong></td> <td>Which DNS servers does the network assign?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Browser or app</strong></td> <td>Does this client use the device resolver or a separate path?</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>VPN or relay</strong></td> <td>Does an active tunnel change where queries go?</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <h2 id="prove-the-filter-works"> <a href="#prove-the-filter-works" title="Prove the Filter Works">Prove the Filter Works</a> <a href="#prove-the-filter-works" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Prove the Filter Works">#</a> </h2> <p>Open your resolver’s query log. Query the chosen blocked domain directly against the filter. On Windows, use PowerShell and enter the filter address and test domain when prompted:</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-powershell" data-lang="powershell"><span style="display:flex;"><span>$filterAddress = Read-Host <span style="color:#e6db74">"Filtering DNS server address"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>$testDomain = Read-Host <span style="color:#e6db74">"Harmless domain blocked by your test rule"</span> </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Resolve-DnsName -Name $testDomain -Server $filterAddress -Type A -DnsOnly </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Microsoft’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Resolve-DnsName reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/dnsclient/resolve-dnsname"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/dnsclient/resolve-dnsname" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" ><strong><code>Resolve-DnsName</code></strong> reference</a> </span> defines <strong><code>-Server</code></strong> as a query to the named resolver. Find the query in the filter log and check the response and matching rule. Pi-hole’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="query and logging documentation"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.pi-hole.net/main/pihole-command/"> <a href="https://docs.pi-hole.net/main/pihole-command/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >query and logging documentation</a> </span> describes its local query tools. If the direct query is allowed, fix the rule or client group assignment before investigating bypass. If the direct query fails to reach the filter, check the address, service, and network path.</p> <p><strong>This direct test does not prove the laptop normally uses the filter.</strong> The <strong><code>-Server</code></strong> option overrides its default resolver for this query. This distinction prevents a common false pass.</p> <h2 id="trace-the-device-path"> <a href="#trace-the-device-path" title="Trace the Device Path">Trace the Device Path</a> <a href="#trace-the-device-path" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Trace the Device Path">#</a> </h2> <p>Use a fresh hostname to avoid a prior DNS cache entry. The following example sends one query directly to the filter and another through the laptop’s normal resolver selection. The names are separate so you know which log entry belongs to each path. An <strong>NXDOMAIN</strong> response means the DNS server reports the hostname does not exist. This response is normal when the random name is unused. The query’s presence in the filter log matters here.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-powershell" data-lang="powershell"><span style="display:flex;"><span>$stamp = [<span style="color:#66d9ef">guid</span>]::NewGuid().ToString(<span style="color:#e6db74">"N"</span>) </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Resolve-DnsName -Name <span style="color:#e6db74">"direct-</span>${stamp}<span style="color:#e6db74">.example.com"</span> -Server $filterAddress -Type A -DnsOnly </span></span><span style="display:flex;"><span>Resolve-DnsName -Name <span style="color:#e6db74">"default-</span>${stamp}<span style="color:#e6db74">.example.com"</span> -Type A -DnsOnly </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Search the filter’s log for both exact names and note the time and reported client. If <strong><code>direct-</code></strong> appears but <strong><code>default-</code></strong> does not, inspect the laptop’s assigned DNS servers. On Windows, <strong><code>Get-DnsClientServerAddress</code></strong> shows DNS server addresses by interface. Check the active Wi-Fi or Ethernet adapter, not a disconnected adapter. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Microsoft’s DNS client reference"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/dnsclient/get-dnsclientserveraddress"> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/dnsclient/get-dnsclientserveraddress" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Microsoft’s DNS client reference</a> </span> defines this read-only command.</p> <p>Leave errors visible during the first test. An error or timeout needs separate diagnosis from an absent query-log entry.</p> <div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" style="color:#f8f8f2;background-color:#272822;-moz-tab-size:4;-o-tab-size:4;tab-size:4;-webkit-text-size-adjust:none;"><code class="language-powershell" data-lang="powershell"><span style="display:flex;"><span>Get-DnsClientServerAddress | Select-Object InterfaceAlias, AddressFamily, ServerAddresses </span></span></code></pre></div><p>Compare IPv4 and IPv6 rows. <strong>DHCP</strong> assigns network settings such as DNS servers. <strong>IPv6</strong> is the newer Internet Protocol address family that uses 128-bit addresses. An IPv4 lease might name the filter while IPv6 router advertisements supply another DNS server. Check the router’s <strong>DHCP</strong> and <strong>IPv6 DNS</strong> advertisements, then renew the device’s network lease after a correction. Pi-hole’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="post-install guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.pi-hole.net/main/post-install/"> <a href="https://docs.pi-hole.net/main/post-install/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >post-install guide</a> </span> explains how DHCP points clients at Pi-hole. Its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="router example"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.pi-hole.net/routers/fritzbox/"> <a href="https://docs.pi-hole.net/routers/fritzbox/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >router example</a> </span> covers IPv6 DNS advertisements.</p> <p>If the log shows the <strong>router</strong> as the client, the router might be forwarding queries on behalf of devices. The filter log then proves the router reached the filter, not which device originated each query. Confirm the router’s forwarding design before treating client identity as missing data.</p> <h2 id="check-browser-dns"> <a href="#check-browser-dns" title="Check Browser DNS">Check Browser DNS</a> <a href="#check-browser-dns" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check Browser DNS">#</a> </h2> <p>A command-line query tests the device resolver path. A browser might use <strong>DNS over HTTPS (DoH)</strong> instead. Open the same blocked test domain in the browser and watch the filter log for a corresponding query. Clear the browser’s DNS cache or use a new hostname under a test rule when cached results obscure the comparison.</p> <p>In <strong>Chrome on a computer</strong>, open <strong>Settings > Privacy and security > Security > Use secure DNS</strong>. Google’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Chrome help"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/10468685?co=GENIE.Platform%3DDesktop&hl=en"> <a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/10468685?co=GENIE.Platform%3DDesktop&hl=en" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Chrome help</a> </span> says automatic mode uses the current provider and falls back to unencrypted lookup on failure. A selected custom provider does not fall back in the same way. Record the selected mode and provider before changing the setting.</p> <p>In <strong>Firefox</strong>, open <strong>Settings > Privacy & Security > DNS over HTTPS</strong>. Mozilla’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="protection-level guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/dns-over-https"> <a href="https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/dns-over-https" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >protection-level guide</a> </span> distinguishes Default, Increased, Max, Custom, and Off modes. Its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DoH overview"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/firefox-dns-over-https"> <a href="https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/firefox-dns-over-https" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >DoH overview</a> </span> explains when a browser resolver bypasses a local DNS filter. Test again after one controlled settings change, then restore your intended privacy setting.</p> <p><strong>Do not label every missing browser query a bypass.</strong> The browser might reuse cached data, reach an already known address, or use a proxy. Compare a fresh name, a matching time window, and the browser’s resolver setting before concluding where the query went.</p> <h2 id="check-mobile-and-vpn-paths"> <a href="#check-mobile-and-vpn-paths" title="Check Mobile and VPN Paths">Check Mobile and VPN Paths</a> <a href="#check-mobile-and-vpn-paths" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Check Mobile and VPN Paths">#</a> </h2> <p>On <strong>Android</strong>, inspect <strong>Settings > Network & internet > Private DNS</strong>. A provider hostname selects a private DNS service distinct from the DNS advertised by your router. Google’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Android network settings"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.google.com/android/answer/9654714?hl=en"> <a href="https://support.google.com/android/answer/9654714?hl=en" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Android network settings</a> </span> explain the Off, Automatic, and provider-hostname choices. Test on Wi-Fi with cellular data disabled for a controlled local result, then restore your normal setting.</p> <p>On <strong>Apple devices</strong>, check whether <strong>iCloud Private Relay</strong> is active for the network and whether Safari uses the path you expect. Apple says <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="Private Relay protects Safari browsing and DNS information"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.apple.com/en-gb/102602"> <a href="https://support.apple.com/en-gb/102602" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >Private Relay protects Safari browsing and DNS information</a> </span> . Its <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="network controls"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://support.apple.com/en-ie/102022"> <a href="https://support.apple.com/en-ie/102022" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >network controls</a> </span> describe per-network handling when filtering conflicts with Private Relay. Do not generalize a Safari result to every app on the device.</p> <p>A <strong>VPN</strong> might supply its own DNS resolver or send queries through the tunnel. Record whether the VPN is connected, its DNS settings, and its split-tunnel policy. Compare the same test with the VPN on and off only if your security policy permits the comparison. A changed result identifies a path difference. The changed result alone does not prove a leak or a filter defect.</p> <h2 id="interpret-the-results"> <a href="#interpret-the-results" title="Interpret the Results">Interpret the Results</a> <a href="#interpret-the-results" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Interpret the Results">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>Evidence</th> <th>Likely next check</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>Direct query absent from filter log</strong></td> <td>Filter address, DNS service, logging, or network reachability</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Direct query allowed</strong></td> <td>Exact deny rule, group policy, or rule priority</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Direct logged, default absent</strong></td> <td>DHCP, static device DNS, IPv6 DNS, or VPN resolver</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Default logged, browser absent</strong></td> <td>Browser DoH, browser cache, proxy, or relay</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>Both logged and blocked, site still loads</strong></td> <td>Another hostname, cached content, direct address, or app path</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p><strong>Missing log entries are ambiguous</strong> when logging is disabled, the router forwards on behalf of the client, or the test reused cached data. Repeat with a fresh hostname and inspect the query time before changing firewall rules. Blocking plain DNS to outside resolvers does not force an encrypted browser or VPN to use your filter. Pi-hole’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="OPNsense guide"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://docs.pi-hole.net/routers/opnsense/"> <a href="https://docs.pi-hole.net/routers/opnsense/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >OPNsense guide</a> </span> presents external-DNS blocking as an optional network control. Device policy and browser configuration remain separate controls.</p> <h2 id="fix-and-retest"> <a href="#fix-and-retest" title="Fix and Retest">Fix and Retest</a> <a href="#fix-and-retest" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Fix and Retest">#</a> </h2> <p>Change one layer at a time. Correct DHCP or IPv6 DNS advertisements, remove an unintended static resolver, select the intended browser DNS provider, or adjust the VPN’s DNS policy. Do not silently weaken encrypted DNS or relay protections across every device to solve one test failure. Record the source device, interface, filter address, queried name, time, response, log client, browser mode, VPN state, and change made.</p> <p>Rerun the <strong>direct</strong>, <strong>default</strong>, and <strong>browser</strong> tests after each change. Keep a fresh hostname for each run. If a device has several network profiles, test each profile separately. The site’s <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DNS resolver comparison"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/dns-comparison-adguard-quad9-cloudflare-pi-hole/"> <a href="/articles/dns-comparison-adguard-quad9-cloudflare-pi-hole/" rel="follow me" >DNS resolver comparison</a> </span> helps choose a service. The <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="browser leak test"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/privacy-browser-leak-test-dns-webrtc/"> <a href="/articles/privacy-browser-leak-test-dns-webrtc/" rel="follow me" >browser leak test</a> </span> addresses a different question: which network information leaves your browser and VPN setup. <strong>A reliable filter result needs a verified rule and a verified client path.</strong></p> <h2 id="next-steps"> <a href="#next-steps" title="Next Steps">Next Steps</a> <a href="#next-steps" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Next Steps">#</a> </h2> <p>Repeat the direct, default, and browser tests after each controlled change. Review the <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="DNS resolver comparison"> <meta itemprop="url" content="/articles/dns-comparison-adguard-quad9-cloudflare-pi-hole/"> <a href="/articles/dns-comparison-adguard-quad9-cloudflare-pi-hole/" rel="follow me" >DNS resolver comparison</a> </span> when selecting a filtering service.</p> Read More at https://simeononsecurity.com/

item.title: 2x RTX 5060 Ti vs GB10: Five-Model Local AI Benchmark at 256K Context
item.description: A five-model RTX 5060 Ti versus GB10 comparison, plus a same-host Qwen3.8 Flash-Next Strata benchmark through 256K context.
item.content:encoded: <p><strong>Two RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB cards provide 32 GB of aggregate VRAM.</strong> An NVIDIA GB10 system provides 128 GB of coherent unified memory. The new five-model benchmark shows a more balanced result than the earlier Qwen-only test.</p> <p>The dual-card system leads on generation speed for four of the five models at the 256K setting. The GB10 leads clearly on Qwen3.8 27B and keeps a larger memory reserve for models, context, and runtime allocations. The best choice depends on the model and workload.</p> <p>A separate same-host run compared Qwen3.8-Flash-Next IQ2_XS on Strata with dense Qwen3.8 27B Q4_K_M on Ollama. The post-warmup generation median was 92.8 tokens per second for Flash-Next with a 260,446-token prompt. Dense Qwen3.8 reached 0.939 tokens per second with a 260,444-token prompt.</p> <p>The NVIDIA GB10 uses 128 GB of coherent unified memory. NVIDIA lists the GB10 platform with 128 GB of LPDDR5x unified memory and a 140 W chip TDP. The RTX 5060 Ti uses 16 GB of GDDR7 per card, a 128-bit memory interface, and a 180 W total graphics power rating. <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti specifications"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/graphics-cards/50-series/rtx-5060-family/"> <a href="https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/graphics-cards/50-series/rtx-5060-family/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >NVIDIA RTX 5060 Ti specifications</a> </span> and <span itemscope itemtype="https://schema.org/WebPage"> <meta itemprop="name" content="NVIDIA GB10 specifications"> <meta itemprop="url" content="https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/"> <a href="https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/" rel="noopener external" target="_blank" >NVIDIA GB10 specifications</a> </span> describe the hardware difference.</p> <p><strong>The two systems do not expose memory in the same way.</strong> Two cards create two separate 16 GB pools. The GB10 places the model, context data, runtime buffers, and operating-system allocations in one shared address space.</p> <h2 id="the-memory-comparison"> <a href="#the-memory-comparison" title="The memory comparison">The memory comparison</a> <a href="#the-memory-comparison" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The memory comparison">#</a> </h2> <table> <thead> <tr> <th>System</th> <th style="text-align: right">Memory</th> <th>Memory model</th> <th style="text-align: right">Reported power figure</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td><strong>2x RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">32 GB aggregate</td> <td>Two separate GPU memory pools</td> <td style="text-align: right">360 W GPU total</td> </tr> <tr> <td><strong>GB10 system</strong></td> <td style="text-align: right">128 GB</td> <td>Coherent unified system memory</td> <td style="text-align: right">140 W GB10 TDP</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>The GB10 does not win every throughput test because LPDDR5x memory matches discrete GPU bandwidth. Its advantage comes from capacity and placement. The CPU and GPU share the same address space, so the working set does not need to fit inside two isolated 16 GB devices.</p> <p>The dual-card system faces a placement problem. The model must split across both cards. The runtime must move data between them. PCIe traffic adds latency and consumes bandwidth. The RTX 5060 Ti also does not support NVLink, according to NVIDIA’s specifications.</p> <h2 id="the-five-model-benchmark"> <a href="#the-five-model-benchmark" title="The five-model benchmark">The five-model benchmark</a> <a href="#the-five-model-benchmark" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="The five-model benchmark">#</a> </h2> <p>The updated run used the same request matrix on both systems. It covered five Ollama models at 4K, 16K, 32K, 64K, 128K, and 256K context settings. Each request generated 128 tokens with temperature 0.</p> <p>The tested model tags were:</p> <ul> <li><strong>Qwen3.8 27B:</strong> <code>qwen3.8:27b</code></li> <li><strong>GPT-OSS 20B:</strong> <code>gpt-oss:20b</code></li> <li><strong>Qwen3.6 35B-A3B:</strong> <code>qwen3.6:35b</code></li> <li><strong>Qwen3.5 35B-A3B:</strong> <code>qwen3.5:35b-a3b-q4_K_M</code></li> <li><strong>Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B:</strong> <code>nemotron-3.5-lightning:30b-a3b-q4_K_M</code></li> </ul> <p>The dual-card system used two RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB cards. The GB10 system used 128 GB of unified memory. The runs used Ollama, with version 0.34.2 on the dual-card system and version 0.40.2 on the GB10 system.</p> <h3 id="generation-speed"> <a href="#generation-speed" title="Generation speed">Generation speed</a> <a href="#generation-speed" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Generation speed">#</a> </h3> <p>Generation speed measures the tokens produced after prompt processing. This metric matters most during an interactive conversation.</p> <p>Dual RTX 5060 Ti system:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th style="text-align: right">Context</th> <th style="text-align: right">GPT-OSS 20B</th> <th style="text-align: right">Nemotron 3.5</th> <th style="text-align: right">Qwen3.5 35B</th> <th style="text-align: right">Qwen3.6 35B</th> <th style="text-align: right">Qwen3.8 27B</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">4K</td> <td style="text-align: right">91.518</td> <td style="text-align: right">162.027</td> <td style="text-align: right">117.547</td> <td right">161.377</td> <td style="text-align: right">112.903</td> <td style="text-align: right">140.596</td> <td style="text-align: right">51.656</td> </tr> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">32K</td> <td style="text-align: right">82.372</td> <td style="text-align: right">157.055</td> <td style="text-align: right">106.455</td> <td style="text-align: right">144.833</td> <td style="text-align: right">130.924</td> <td style="text-align: right">79.572</td> <td style="text-align: right">115.352</td> <td style="text-align: right">26.399</td> </tr> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">256K</td> <td style="text-align: right">67.853</td> <td style="text-align: right">106.221</td> <td style="text-align: right">58.947</td> <td style="text-align: right">67.159</td> <td style="text-align: right">1.079</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>GB10:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th style="text-align: right">Context</th> <th style="text-align: right">GPT-OSS 20B</th> <th style="text-align: right">100.906</td> <td style="text-align: right">32.985</td> </tr> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">16K</td> <td style="text-align: right">56.764</td> <td style="text-align: right">94.366</td> <td style="text-align: right">69.782</td> <td style="text-align: right">95.448</td> <td style="text-align: right">32.939</td> </tr> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">32K</td> <td style="text-align: right">53.257</td> <td style="text-align: right">98.175</td> <td style="text-align: right">64.055</td> <td style="text-align: right">95.025</td> <td style="text-align: right">29.772</td> </tr> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">64K</td> <td style="text-align: right">49.201</td> <td style="text-align: right">96.132</td> <td style="text-align: right">58.428</td> <td style="text-align: right">84.528</td> <td style="text-align: right">25.625</td> </tr> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">128K</td> <td style="text-align: right">40.637</td> <td style="text-align: right">80.238</td> <td style="text-align: right">48.108</td> <td style="text-align: right">74.579</td> <td style="text-align: right">22.294</td> </tr> <tr> <td style="text-align: right">256K</td> <td style="text-align: right">43.688</td> <td style="text-align: right">68.043</td> <td style="text-align: right">36.649</td> <td style="text-align: right">62.115</td> <td style="text-align: right">22.371</td> </tr> </tbody> </table> <p>At 256K, the dual-card system generated faster on GPT-OSS, Nemotron, Qwen3.5, and Qwen3.6. The GB10 generated faster on Qwen3.8 by a wide margin. Qwen3.8 dropped to 1.079 tokens per second on the dual-card system while the GB10 produced 22.371 tokens per second.</p> <p>The Qwen3.6 result is close. The dual-card system reached 67.159 tokens per second and the GB10 reached 62.115. The result does not support a universal claim that unified memory always wins or that two discrete GPUs always win.</p> <h3 id="prompt-processing-speed"> <a href="#prompt-processing-speed" title="Prompt processing speed">Prompt processing speed</a> <a href="#prompt-processing-speed" class="h-anchor" aria-hidden="true" title="Prompt processing speed">#</a> </h3> <p>Prompt processing measures how fast the runtime reads the input context before generation. It matters for long documents and repeated context reloads.</p> <p>Dual RTX 5060 Ti system:</p> <table> <thead> <tr> <th style="text-align: right">Context</th> <th style="text-align: right">GPT-OSS 20B</th> <th style="text-align: right">Nemotron 3.5</th> <th style="text-align: right">Qwen3.5 35B</th> <th style="text-align: right">Qwen3.6 35B</th> <th style="text-align: right">Qwen3.8 27B</th> style="text-align: right">5838.3</td> <td style="text-align: right">1813.2</td> <td style="text-align: right">2229.1</td> <td style="text-align: right">1011.0</td> <td style="text-align: right">Nemotron 3.5</th> <th style="text-align: right">Qwen3.5 35B</th> <th style="text-align: right">Qwen3.6 35B</th> <th style="text-align: right">Qwen3.8 27B</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td
